Even once the parser stopped corrupting it, the single Cell.runs field had nowhere to put "text after the table" separately from "text before the table" — fill_tables always inserted a cell's text at its first paragraph, i.e. always immediately before any nested table, regardless of where the text actually appeared in the source HTML. Filed as follow-up #275 rather than silently expanding #108's scope; then, per explicit direction, fixed in the same pass ("do the fuller version").

docs.title: Schema change (ast.py)
docs.text: Cell.runs: list[Run] + Cell.nested_table: Table | None → Cell.children: list[Run | Table] — one ordered list holding exactly what appeared in the source, in order. This is the Union[Run, Table] design #92 originally proposed and explicitly didn't ship; the simpler two-field version turned out to be insufficient once #275 surfaced.

docs.title: Parser changes (html_parser.py)
docs.text: _TableBuilder replaces _current_nested_table/_pending_leading_runs with a single _current_children: list[Run | Table], plus append_runs()/append_nested_table() methods that append to it in call order. _AstParser.handle_starttag's table branch flushes pending runs onto the outer builder via append_runs() before pushing a new builder for the nested table (fixing defect 1 above); handle_endtag's table branch calls append_nested_table() on the parent builder instead of setting a single field. end_cell builds Cell(children=self._current_children + runs, ...). This works at arbitrary depth and for arbitrarily many nested tables per cell — no explicit depth/count limit needed.

docs.title: Emitter changes (emitter.py)
docs.text:
Cells with no Table in children are still filled in one bulk batch by _build_fill_requests (unchanged, fast path — most cells). Cells with at least one Table child go through a new recursive, round-based algorithm:

  • _fill_children_recursive(docs_service, doc_id, resolve, ast_tables) — resolve(live_doc) -> doc_table dicts positionally matching ast_tables. Tracks a per-cell cursor into children. Each round: for every still-pending cell, emit one contiguous segment — either a run of text (insertText + styles) or one nested table's shell (insertTable) — at that cell's next open position, sorted high→low within the round (same pattern as the old phase-3/5 code), then re-fetch before the next round.
  • _cell_para_start_for_cursor: a cell's content alternates paragraph/table/paragraph/table/...; the Nth paragraph (0-indexed) is the one after the Nth already-inserted table, where N = count of Table children before cursor.
  • _text_offset_since_last_table: a table's insertion point is its paragraph's startIndex plus this — the length of any text already inserted into that same paragraph earlier in this round-chain (the paragraph's own startIndex doesn't change when text is inserted into it, but the table must land after that text, not at the start).
  • When a table shell is inserted, _fill_table_fully is called for it: re-fetches, bulk-fills its own plain cells via _build_fill_requests, then recurses via _fill_children_recursive for any of its cells that themselves contain a further nested table. This is what makes nesting depth unbounded — a nested table is filled exactly the same way a top-level one is.
  • After recursing into any nested tables inserted in a round (which run their own batchUpdates and shift subsequent document indices), the outer loop re-fetches again before its own next round — recursion's mutations must be visible before the outer cell's next segment (e.g. trailing text) is positioned.
  • _ast_cell_to_doc_cell / _find_nth_table_in_cell locate a specific physical doc cell / the Nth nested-table content element inside a cell, reusing the existing _physical_to_ast_indices/_build_phantom_set colspan/rowspan-aware mapping.

_build_nested_table_inserts and _collect_nested_table_pairs (the old phase-3/5 helpers) are removed — fully superseded by the recursive algorithm.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
• Text before, between, and after any number of nested tables in one cell renders in true source order, at any nesting depth.
  • The "one level of nesting only" and "no colspan/rowspan/col_widths inside nested tables" limitations from the original #92 design are otherwise unchanged — this rewrite only touches content ordering, not those structural features.
  • Tested with tests/test_docs_tables.py's TestFillNestedCellContent, which drives the real algorithm against a small in-memory Docs-API simulator (FakeDoc/Para/TableNode in that file) that actually applies insertText/insertTable mutations and re-derives indices — chosen over hand-computed index fixtures because this much re-fetch/recursion logic is easy to get subtly wrong in a way a fixture can't catch (and did, twice, during development).

docs.title: Nested table colspan/rowspan (#109)
docs.text:
Date: 2026-07-08

Nested tables produced a correctly-sized shell but never merged cells with colspan/rowspan > 1 — _fill_table_fully (the per-nested-table fill helper introduced in the rewrite above) only ran the plain-cell bulk fill, with no equivalent of the outer-table merge phase (fill_tables phase 2).

Fix: _fill_table_fully now checks the nested ast_table for any cell with colspan > 1 or rowspan > 1 and, if found, builds and executes mergeTableCells requests via the existing _build_merge_requests (unchanged — it already operated generically on any doc_table/ast_table pair, nested or not) before re-fetching and running the bulk fill. This exactly mirrors fill_tables's own phase 1→2→3 order, just scoped to one nested table.

col_widths on nested tables remains unsupported — out of scope for #109, not addressed here.

Tested in tests/test_docs_tables.py's TestNestedTableMerges, extending the same FakeDoc simulator with a no-op mergeTableCells handler (the real Docs API doesn't shift indices or delete content on merge — covered cells stay physical, just skipped by the existing phantom-cell mapping — so the simulator has nothing to mutate; the tests instead assert the merge request's shape and its position in batch order relative to the fill).

docs.title: Design: effectiveFormat spike — cell formatting assertions via API
docs.text:
Date: 2026-06-20 Issue: #54 Status: complete

Point-in-time spike. Confirms that formatting applied via batch_update is fully readable back through get_sheet_data(include_grid_data=True), without a browser.

docs.title: What we tested
docs.text:
Applied three separate formats to fixture cells using batch_update → repeatCell: 1. Bold on A1 (text cell) 2. Italic + background color on B1 (text cell) 3. Currency number format on B2 (numeric cell)

Then read back via get_sheet_data(spreadsheet_id, sheet="Sales", range="A1:B2", include_grid_data=True).

docs.title: Response shape
docs.text:
Each cell object under sheets[0].data[0].rowData[row].values[col] has:

{
  userEnteredValue:  { stringValue | numberValue | boolValue | formulaValue }
  effectiveValue:    { stringValue | numberValue | ... }   # post-formula
  formattedValue:    "..."                                  # display string
  userEnteredFormat: { ... }                               # what was explicitly set
  effectiveFormat: {
    backgroundColor:      { red, green, blue }
    backgroundColorStyle: { rgbColor: { red, green, blue } }
    padding:              { top, right, bottom, left }
    horizontalAlignment:  "LEFT" | "CENTER" | "RIGHT"
    verticalAlignment:    "TOP" | "MIDDLE" | "BOTTOM"
    wrapStrategy:         "OVERFLOW_CELL" | "WRAP" | "CLIP"
    hyperlinkDisplayType: "PLAIN_TEXT" | "LINKED"
    numberFormat:         { type, pattern }               # only if set
    textFormat: {
      fontFamily:      "Arial"
      fontSize:        10
      bold:            false
      italic:          false
      strikethrough:   false
      underline:       false
      foregroundColor: { red, green, blue }               # {} means default (black)
      foregroundColorStyle: { rgbColor: { ... } }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: What is assertable
docs.text: Field Confirmed Notes effectiveFormat.textFormat.bold ✅ true/false effectiveFormat.textFormat.italic ✅ true/false effectiveFormat.textFormat.underline ✅ in schema; not separately tested effectiveFormat.textFormat.strikethrough ✅ in schema; not separately tested effectiveFormat.textFormat.fontSize ✅ integer effectiveFormat.textFormat.fontFamily ✅ string effectiveFormat.textFormat.foregroundColor ✅ RGB — see float note below effectiveFormat.backgroundColor ✅ RGB — see float note below effectiveFormat.horizontalAlignment ✅ LEFT for text, RIGHT for numbers by default effectiveFormat.verticalAlignment ✅ string effectiveFormat.wrapStrategy ✅ string effectiveFormat.numberFormat.type ✅ CURRENCY, PERCENT, DATE, etc. effectiveFormat.numberFormat.pattern ✅ format string formattedValue ✅ rendered display string — simplest way to assert number format

docs.title: RGB float precision
docs.text:
The API returns RGB as floats in [0, 1]. 0.9 is transmitted as 0.8980392 (229/255 rounded). When asserting colors, use approximate matching (± 1/255 ≈ 0.004), or compare round(v * 255) as integers.

Example: {red:1, green:0.9, blue:0.6} comes back as {red:1, green:0.8980392, blue:0.6}.

docs.title: Fixture strategy
docs.text:
The fixture spreadsheet has no pre-applied formatting (all cells use spreadsheet defaults). Formatting tests follow a setup→assert→teardown pattern:

  1. Setup: batch_update with repeatCell to apply the format to target cells.
  2. Assert: get_sheet_data(include_grid_data=True, range=<target>) and inspect effectiveFormat.
  3. Teardown: batch_update with repeatCell { cell: {}, fields: "userEnteredFormat" } to clear all custom formatting from those cells.

This keeps the fixture clean between tests and avoids needing a dedicated "Formatting" sheet.

docs.title: Safe-by-Default Gmail Sending
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-25 Issue: #1081 (spec revised from the design pass in its thread). Follow-ups: #1235 (confirming on 2026-07-28 connections), #1236 (the same capability-only check in the OAuth re-authorization offer).

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: send_message, reply_to_message and send_draft delivered mail immediately, guarded only by destructiveHint. Clients treat that as a hint and skip it once a tool is auto-approved, and an instruction in the prompt can be lost when an agent's context is compacted. So the gate has to be in the server.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
GMAIL_SEND=confirm (the default) never delivers on the agent's call alone:

  1. send_message and reply_to_message compose the message as before, then save it with drafts.create instead of messages.send. A reply carries the original's threadId, so the held draft sits in the thread.
  2. Every send then goes through _confirm_and_send_draft, which send_draft uses too:
  3. It reads the draft back (drafts.get(format="full")) and builds the confirmation from the stored message. Gmail stamps the draft's From when storing it (checked live), so the form shows the real sender, not the tool's arguments.
  4. It computes recipient flags (_recipient_flags) from the stored To/Cc/Bcc.
  5. If the call can't elicit (_can_elicit_form), it returns the held-draft result.
  6. Otherwise it asks through ctx.elicit with a one-field form (send: bool, required, no default), bounded by _CONFIRM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS.
  7. Only an accepted form with send true continues. It re-reads the draft (format="minimal") and sends with drafts.send({"id": draft_id}) only if the message ID matches the one the form was built from.
  8. Every other outcome returns {"sent": false, "reason", "draft_id", "message", "recipient_flags", "note"}. The reasons are no_elicitation, declined, cancelled, timeout, error, and changed.

GMAIL_SEND=direct keeps the old code paths unchanged. The only change there is that results gain sent: true, so both modes share one result shape.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Draft first, then ask. The draft exists before the question, so every non-yes outcome, including a cancelled tool call or a dropped connection mid-form, leaves something the user can find in Gmail. Asking first and composing after would lose the message on every refusal.

Detection needs can_send_request. On an MCP 2026-07-28 connection, mcp 2.3.0 still reports the client's form capability, but session.can_send_request is False and ctx.elicit raises NoBackChannelError (probed in the design pass, and confirmed again by this PR's in-process mcp.Client(mode="2026-07-28") test and live run). A capability-only check, like reauth._supports_url_elicitation, would elicit and fail. A bare elicitation: {} counts as form support, matching mcp's own _require_capability.

NoBackChannelError is caught in the tool. It's an MCPError, so letting it propagate would end the call as a protocol error and lose draft_id. It's the backstop for a channel that drops between the check and the request. In this PR's own tests it also covered the 2026-07-28 path when the can_send_request check was removed as a mutation check.

Confirmed content = sent content, by message ID. drafts.update replaces a draft's message ID and keeps its draft ID (checked live before implementing: one update_draft gave the draft a new message ID under the same draft ID). So the message ID recorded at confirmation identifies what the user saw, and the hash fallback the spec allowed wasn't needed. drafts.send has no precondition, so the check is a separate read, and a short window remains (docs/known-limitations.md). send_draft keeps draft_id as its only argument, since drafts.send also accepts replacement content.

The form treats the draft as untrusted. The agent being guarded against writes the draft, so nothing in it may change what the form appears to say (PR #1249 QA round 1). Body text sits under a Body (first 500 of N characters): label with every line prefixed │. Subject, names and filenames are flattened to one line. The HTML part, which recipients' mail apps show instead of the plain text, is rendered as text and shown too, unless it reads the same. Addresses are shown decoded rather than through formataddr, which re-encodes non-ASCII names as RFC 2047 and raises on a non-ASCII address.

Organization = the primary address's domain plus non-consumer alias domains. _own_addresses now also records gmail_primary_address (isPrimary from sendAs.list, else getProfile). A consumer primary (gmail.com, googlemail.com) turns the outside-organization flag off. Keying it on "any alias is a consumer domain" instead would wrongly disable the flag for a Workspace user with an external send-as alias. For the same reason, a consumer alias domain isn't added to the organization set: a personal gmail.com alias would otherwise hide the flag for every gmail.com recipient (PR #1249 QA round 1). An unknown primary returns outside_organization_unchecked instead of an empty list, so the result never implies every recipient is inside.

Unrecognized GMAIL_SEND falls back to confirm. A typo should fail safe, not send.

docs.title: Not done here
docs.text: Confirming on 2026-07-28 connections through the InputRequiredResult round trip is #1235. On those connections mail stays a draft.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Markdown converted from GitHub/GitLab Pages-published source uses standard heading-anchor links for internal cross-references, e.g. [Appendix A](#appendix-a---approved-hashing-algorithms). These are meaningful on the source site (which auto-generates heading slugs), but after create_doc/create_doc_from_file/write_doc_content conversion, the run keeps the literal #slug fragment as its link_url — a URL fragment that means nothing inside a Google Doc. The link renders as a normal blue/underlined hyperlink but goes nowhere, which reads as an error to anyone reviewing the document (worse than plain, unlinked text).

docs.title: What actually resolves it
docs.text:
Google Docs has its own internal-link mechanism, and the issue originally assumed it required the Link.headingId/Link.bookmarkId API fields. Live testing (2026-07-24, see the issue thread) found a simpler path: a Doc's own "Copy link to heading" feature produces an ordinary HTTPS URL — https://docs.google.com/document/d/<docId>/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.<hash> — and setting that as a normal link_url via style_doc_range works as a real in-doc jump link. No special Link object field is needed.

The only missing piece was discovering a heading's h.xxx id. It turns out to already be present in every documents.get() response (paragraphStyle.headingId), confirmed live against both TITLE/SUBTITLE and HEADING_1..6 paragraphs — no includeTabsContent flag or tabs-aware restructuring needed, since the default single-tab response already carries the field. get_doc_structure now surfaces it.

docs.title: The harder problem: which anchor names which heading
docs.text:
Knowing a heading's real id isn't enough — resolving #appendix-a---approved-hashing-algorithms back to the "Appendix A - Approved Hashing Algorithms" heading requires reproducing whichever slugification algorithm the source site used to generate that anchor in the first place, and that information isn't recorded anywhere in the markdown itself.

GitHub's and GitLab's conventions differ in one concrete way: GitHub does not collapse consecutive hyphens produced by adjacent whitespace and a literal hyphen (" - " → "---", confirmed against this issue's own real anchor); GitLab/Kramdown-style conventions do collapse them. Rather than trying to detect which generator produced a given document up front (usually not knowable, and for most ordinary headings the two conventions agree anyway — they only diverge on this hyphen-collapsing edge case), anchors.py tries both schemes against the document's own real heading list and accepts whichever produces an exact match. The GitLab-style scheme is delegated to python-markdown's own toc extension slugify (already a project dependency, confirmed live to collapse hyphens the same way); GitHub's non-collapsing convention has no known off-the-shelf Python equivalent, so it's hand-rolled.

A normalized word-token comparison is the last-resort fallback for a slug that doesn't exactly match either scheme but clearly names the same heading — e.g. the heading was reworded slightly after the source anchors were generated. It tries the anchor's tokens literally first (a trailing -<digits> could be genuine heading wording, not a dedup suffix — unconditionally stripping it caused PR #453's own QA round to catch a wrong-heading resolution); only if that fails, and the anchor does end in digits, is the suffix treated as a duplicate-occurrence index and used to pick the matching heading at that specific occurrence — never just "the first match" once duplicates are in play, and never a guess when the claimed occurrence doesn't exist.

Known limitation, flagged inline (anchors.py, TODO(#409 follow-up)): this is a cascading try-each-scheme-then-fall-back approach — a reasonable first pass, not the most precise or efficient possible mechanism. A more targeted design might resolve the scheme once per document (from the first anchor that disambiguates it) rather than re-deriving every scheme's full slug list per anchor. Revisit if this becomes a real cost or accuracy problem in practice.

docs.title: Product decision: an opinionated layer, not just a primitive
docs.text:
The original ask could have been satisfied by exposing headingId and leaving matching to the calling agent (construct the URL, decide which heading an anchor means, call style_doc_range itself). That was deliberately rejected in favor of resolving anchors automatically as part of the conversion pipeline (create_doc/create_doc_from_file/ write_doc_content), for a fixed cost in code size:

  • Consistency at lower agent cost. An agent converting a policy document with a dozen internal cross-references gets working links for free, with zero extra tool calls or per-link reasoning, instead of having to fetch the structure, match anchors to headings itself, and construct the (undocumented) jump-link URL format by hand for every single link.
  • A wrong link is worse than no link. An anchor that matches no heading with reasonable confidence gets its link stripped (text kept, plain) rather than left dangling or guessed — matching the issue's own "at minimum" fallback ask. A dead-looking link reads as an error; a link that silently points at the wrong section is actively misleading.
  • headingId still surfaces on get_doc_structure as a byproduct (same underlying read the resolution pass needs internally) — the escape hatch stays open for cases the automatic layer doesn't cover: docs not produced by markdown/HTML conversion through this project, or an agent building something custom (a live table of contents, cross-reference audit, etc.).

This "prefer an opinionated server-side layer over exposing raw primitives, when it produces consistent results at lower agent cost" framing is a standing design principle for this project going forward — noted here as the concrete precedent, not restated as a general rule elsewhere in this repo.

docs.title: Scope not covered here
docs.text:
• Tabs. Every tool in this codebase (including the new resolution pass) operates only against a document's default tab (t.0) — the constructed jump-link URL hardcodes tab=t.0. No tool surface is tabs-aware today; that's a separate, not-yet-filed concern flagged in the issue thread, not part of this fix.
  • Duplicate-heading disambiguation order. The -1, -2, ... suffix convention is applied in document order per slugification scheme, matching how GitHub/GitLab number repeated headings — but if a document was heavily edited after the source anchors were generated (headings reordered, renamed, or added), the disambiguation numbering can drift out of sync with the original source's numbering. The fuzzy fallback does not attempt to recover this case; an anchor whose exact numbered slug no longer matches falls through to being stripped.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: create_doc/create_doc_from_file/write_doc_content silently dropped every <img> / ![alt](src) during conversion (confirmed via TC-DOC102/103, filed as the original #333 bug report). The only path to an embedded image was the pre-existing insert_local_images (#332), which requires a manual placeholder-marker workaround per image — a multi-step, multi-tool-call dance the issue's own reporter described in detail.

docs.title: Image as a first-class AST node, not a marker
docs.text:
The tempting shortcut was to reuse insert_local_images's already-proven marker mechanism under the hood: substitute each ![]() with a unique placeholder token during markdown→HTML conversion, let the existing (unmodified) AST/emitter pipeline treat it as ordinary text, then run a second pass after the main content batch to locate each marker and swap in the image — exactly what insert_local_images already does. This would have meant zero changes to ast.py/html_parser.py/emitter.py's position math.

Rejected in favor of a true Image AST node (ast.py) because the marker approach requires a second round-trip after the main insertText/table batch — a real robustness cost (a doc left with literal marker text visible if the second pass fails) for no benefit once the atomic single-batch approach turned out to be achievable. An Image node contributes zero characters to ast_to_requests's text-building pass (unlike a marker) — it's purely a positional marker within a node's runs list, resolved into its own insertInlineImage request. This lets it piggyback on the exact "process positional insertions in descending-document-order" pattern this codebase already uses for tables (ast_to_requests's trailing loop), generalized here into positional_inserts: a single combined list of (final_position, request) covering both tables and images, sorted descending and applied together. Interleaving them in one list (not two separate blocks, "all tables then all images") matters — a table inserted before a lower-position image within the same document would otherwise physically shift that image's precomputed position before it gets a chance to run.

ast_to_requests stays fully synchronous (no network I/O) by taking an image_uris: dict[id(image), str] map rather than doing any resolution itself. An Image with no entry in that map is silently omitted — the same graceful-degradation behavior any other unsupported construct already gets from this parser.

Since #1240, content._convert_doc_content builds the requests before any image resolves, so a conversion that fails or is cancelled never reaches the doc. It collects every Image with extract_images(nodes) and passes a unique placeholder URI for each one. _apply_doc_content then resolves the images and swaps each resolved image's placeholder for its real URI. An unresolved image's insertInlineImage request is replaced by its fallback text (below), and its link request goes, since the fallback carries the link. Its insert sits in the descending-position tail, so text at that position shifts none of the requests still to come (test_unresolved_images_requests_match_their_fallback_text pins this).

docs.title: Fallback text for an image that isn't embedded (#1099)
docs.text:
An image Docs can't embed used to disappear: an SVG badge (img.shields.io serves SVG, which Docs doesn't take), an unreachable URL, a missing local file, a failed share. A README's badge line became an empty paragraph, its link gone too. Now emitter.image_fallback_requests writes image_fallback_text(image) where the image would have gone: its alt text with whitespace collapsed, else the last segment of its source (a URL's path segment, percent-decoded; a local path's file name, never the whole path, so a server path doesn't land in the doc; nothing for a drive: ID), else image. Alt text that's empty wouldn't help a reader find what's missing.

  • One request pair, either way. An insertText at the image's position, then an updateTextStyle with fields: "link": the image's link (through _storable_link_url, the text-link rule), or, for an unlinked image, cleared. Inserted text takes the style of the character before it, a link included, which an inserted image never does (#977). Its other inherited styles stay, so it reads like the text around it.
  • Where it applies. An image that didn't resolve (_apply_doc_content, before the first batch), and one Docs couldn't fetch at the embed step (_drop_failed_image in the body, CellImages._drop in cells), which now replace the failed insert in place instead of popping it. Either way the text goes at the image's own position in the descending tail, so no request after it moves, the same argument that made dropping safe.
  • The K≥2 split. _positional_insert_tail_start takes the fallback requests' ids (fallback_ids), so a fallback inside the tail doesn't cut the scan short and fall back to whole-list retries.
  • Reporting. The image's images entry keeps its error and gains fallback_text once the batch carrying the text has landed: send_dropping_failed_images's on_applied for the body, and CellImages.shown_as_text for cells. A batch that fails for another reason leaves it out.
  • Not in a heading (PR #1310 QA round 1). The anchor pass reads a heading's text from its runs, so fallback text there joins the heading's own: # MyProj ![build](svg) became "MyProj build", and [Go](#myproj) lost its link (no_matching_heading). GitHub leaves image alt text out of a slug, so a README's TOC is written against the heading without it. An image in any paragraph the anchor pass reads as a heading (any named style but NORMAL_TEXT: Heading, a BulletItem with heading_level, a TITLE/SUBTITLE NamedBlock; emitter.heading_image_ids, recorded on ConvertedContent.heading_image_ids) is dropped as before #1099, with its link request, and reported by its error alone.
  • One tracker. emitter.ImageFallbacks builds every fallback (computing each image's text once), records its request ids for the tail scan, and moves an image into shown from the on_applied of the batch that carried it. The body's retry and CellImages share the one instance _apply_doc_content makes, so both report fallback_text the same way.
  • Source kinds. ast.image_source_kind is the one classification (URL, drive:, data:, local path), used by _resolve_image_source, the replace's folder check, and the fallback text. A data: URI (markdown-it lets data:image/... through) is an error, since Docs takes an image only by URL, and its fallback is its alt or "image", never its base64. A protocol-relative //host/... (host starting with a letter or digit, the link rule from #1180) is a URL, fetched over https (ast.image_url). html_parser._image_src strips the src once, when the Image is built, so src=" https://..." isn't read as a local path (PR #1310 QA round 2).
  • What it doesn't cover. insert_inline_image and insert_local_images insert one image the caller named at an index, and still fail outright: there's no source text to stand in for.

docs.title: Where a local image comes from and goes (#1121, #1139)
docs.text:
• Relative paths. create_doc_from_file and update_doc_from_file pass the file's folder as source_dir, and _local_image_path joins a relative src to it, as a README's images are relative to the README. It's the caller's spelling of the folder (Path(local_path).parent), not the resolved one, so a symlinked file's images are found next to the link. The joined path goes through check_read like any other (#796). _find_local_image tries the path as written, then percent-decoded: markdown-it keeps images/my%20diagram.png as written, and GitHub resolves it to images/my diagram.png; as written goes first, so a file whose name really holds a % still wins (PR #1310 QA round 2). Content passed as a string (create_doc, write_doc_content, upload_file) has no file, so a relative path there stays relative to the server's working directory.
  • Upload folder. A local image goes to folder_id (the tool's, else the server's default), else the doc's own folder (_image_folder). For the create tools that's the new doc's parent, which Drive reports even for My Drive's root. For the replace tools (write_doc_content, update_doc_from_file, which now take folder_id too), _replace_doc_content looks the doc's parents up only when the content has a local image this server would upload and no folder was given (_uploadable_local_image: the access policy allows reading it and it's a file). A doc shared from a folder the account can't see has no parents, and a failed lookup (a 403, a 5xx) has none to offer: either way the call refuses with {"error", "docId"} before the backup copy and the clear, since replacing would drop every such image. That lookup is the replace's first read of the doc, so a 404, or a 403 that isn't a rate limit (_doc_unreachable), is reported as the doc being unreachable, not as a missing folder (PR #1310 QA round 2) (the #1139 report: a successful call that left the doc without its images). A local image that can't be read anyway (missing, or refused by LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS) doesn't cause the refusal: a folder wouldn't help it, and it's written as its alt text (PR #1310 QA round 1).
  • One body for the create tools. create_doc_from_file calls _create_doc_with_content with source_dir, like create_doc and upload_file, so the image-folder fallback lives in one place.

docs.title: Three source kinds, one shared resolver
docs.text:
src may be a local filesystem path (uploaded to Drive, then shared), a drive:<file_id> reference to an already-uploaded file (shared, not uploaded), or a public http(s):// URL (used directly — no upload, no share, nothing to revoke). _resolve_image_source (content.py) implements all three; insert_local_images's own upload+share logic was left as its existing inline code rather than refactored to share this helper, since its local-path-only case doesn't need the source-kind dispatch.

Local-path and drive: sources are shared anyone:reader regardless of source, since the Docs backend fetches an inline image as an anonymous HTTP request at insertion time — confirmed live in #332, reconfirmed here for the drive: case specifically. Per explicit product decision (2026-08-02), that temporary share is revoked again by default once the image is actually embedded (revoke_sharing=True) — a behavior change from #332's insert_local_images, which always left images shared with no flag at all; both surfaces now share the same default and the same opt-out flag, since a caller has no principled reason to want different defaults from two tools performing the same upload→share→embed→[revoke] lifecycle.

docs.title: Live-discovered bug: one bad image URI fails the entire batch
docs.text:
The atomic single-batch design (image + table insertions bundled with all other content requests) has a real failure mode the position-math design alone doesn't cover: the Docs API rejects an entire batchUpdate if any one insertInlineImage request in it can't be fetched by Google's own (unauthenticated, separate-network-path) image-fetching service — confirmed live via TC-DOC102's own Case 8 (a deliberately unreachable URL), which was silently killing Cases 1–5's otherwise-valid image requests in the same call. This is not a position-math bug — a rejected batchUpdate executes nothing at all, successful or not.

Fixed by treating this as a retryable, not fatal, failure: Google's own error message names the failing request's index directly ("Invalid requests[N].insertInlineImage: ..."), so _apply_doc_content catches the HttpError, parses that index out of the structured response (_failed_insert_image_request_index — status 400 plus HttpError.reason, which the client library fills from the JSON body's error.message, not HttpError's own display string, #510), and strips exactly that request (since #1099, replaces it with the image's fallback text; see below). The dropped image's outcome error is built from that same field, minus its Invalid requests[N]. lead-in (N indexes an internal retry batch). Safe without any position recomputation specifically because a rejected batch never partially applies — every other request's absolute position is exactly as valid on retry as it was on the first attempt. The removed image's outcome entry gets an error field; every other image/table/text request in the same call is unaffected.

Google names only the first failing image per error (confirmed live), so K unreachable images need K retries. Resending the whole document each time would be K+1 full-size round trips, so (#510):

  • K=0 and K=1 stay all-or-nothing. The happy path is one atomic call; the first retry is still one atomic call of the whole remaining list. K=1, the common case, costs 2 calls, the same as before #510.
  • From the second bad image on, the list splits at the start of ast_to_requests's trailing descending-position insertTable/insertInlineImage pass (_positional_insert_tail_start). The prefix (text, styles, bullets) is committed once on its own, and only the small tail is retried per further bad image. That boundary is the only safe split point: every prefix request must run before any positional insert, while within the tail each insert lands at or before every insert already applied, so dropping one never shifts the rest.
  • Residual partial-write window (K≥2 only): once the prefix has committed, a tail retry that fails for a non-image reason raises with the text already in the doc but no tables or images, and fill_tables never runs.
  • Fail-safe: the tail boundary is inferred from request kinds, so it silently depends on ast_to_requests emitting nothing after its positional-insert pass (pinned by a unit test). If any image request is found outside the inferred tail, the retry never splits and falls back to whole-list retries.

Confirmed live that the split produces a document structurally identical to the old whole-list retry (text, bullets, table, and the surviving image all in place).

docs.title: Linked images (#977)
docs.text:
An <img> inside <a href> (markdown [![alt](src)](url)) keeps its link: html_parser.py copies the open <a>'s href onto Image.link_url. That includes raw HTML with no enclosing block: a top-level <img> gets an implicit paragraph even when it's wrapped in inline tags (unlike bare text or <hr> in that position), and reads its link from _bare_link_url, a stack separate from _link_url so text handling and an unclosed top-level <a> are unaffected. Each open <a> records which of the two stacks it pushed onto, or that it pushed nothing (_anchor_pushes), and its </a> pops only that: an href-less <a name> nested in a linked anchor used to pop the outer link (#994, PR #992 QA round 2). Docs stores an image's link on its inlineObjectElement's own textStyle.link, so emitter.py follows the image's insertInlineImage with an updateTextStyle over its one-character range [position, position + 1). The link has to come right after its own insert, inside the descending-position tail: at that point nothing before position has shifted yet. An inserted image never inherits a neighboring run's link (confirmed live, both directions), so an unlinked image gets no clearing request.

Inserts that share a position, such as adjacent images with nothing between them, each land in front of whatever is already there, so the later one in the document has to be inserted first. The descending pass sorts on (position, node order, item order), all descending; sorting by position alone kept source order within a tie and wrote adjacent images reversed (PR #992 QA round 1). A table and the image right after it share a position the same way, and still come out table first.

The retry treats the pair as one unit. ast_to_requests(image_links=...) records each id(insert request) -> link request as it builds them, and _apply_doc_content uses that record rather than matching request shapes. _drop_failed_image pops the link request with its failed insert, since a stranded link would land on whatever character now sits at that position. _positional_insert_tail_start counts a recorded link request as part of the tail, so the K≥2 split still applies. A #slug image link goes through the heading-anchor pass like a text link: _walk_headings_and_anchor_runs reads the inlineObjectElement's link too, so it's resolved or stripped.

docs.title: 333 shipped body-level images only: the parser dropped an <img> in a cell, with no error and
docs.text:
no images entry. Table cells aren't written in phase 1. fill_tables fills them afterwards from live indices, so a cell image goes in during that fill, not in ast_to_requests's positional pass.

  • Parser. An <img> in a cell joins Cell.children in source order, with its <a> link, the same as in a block. A nested <table> already flushed the open cell's pending runs into the outer cell before it started, so an image keeps its place on either side of a nested table. A run of whitespace holding a line break at a segment's edge (the cell's start or end, or either side of a nested table, as in <td>\n Intro\n <table>) is dropped, whether its text chunk is whitespace-only or not; kept, it became empty paragraphs around a nested table (PR #1215 QA rounds 1 and 3). At the segment's start it's dropped as it arrives. At the end of the text so far it's held, as a run with the style and link it was typed under, and written only if more content follows, so everything else in a cell parses as before. Nothing inside a cell's <pre> is trimmed. Collapsing every source line break instead (round 1's fix) merged a cell's <p>s and a <pre>'s lines, which Docs keeps as separate lines (round 2). Whether a newline inside cell text should collapse as a browser renders it is #1221.
  • Resolution. extract_images walks cells too, nested tables included, in document order. Cell images are uploaded, shared and revoked with the body's, through the same ImageShareLifecycle, and get the same images entries.
  • Placement. The fill gets the resolved URIs as an emitter.CellImages. Each contiguous run of a cell's text and images (_run_group_fill_requests) inserts its text and styles as if no image were there, then each image at the offset of the text before it, latest first, like the body's descending pass. Images that share an offset (no text between them) therefore come out in source order, and none shifts another. A linked image's updateTextStyle follows its insert, as in the body.
  • Nested tables. A nested table goes in at its paragraph's start plus everything already inserted before it in that paragraph, so _text_offset_since_last_table counts what each image took (CellImages.doc_length): one index for an embedded image, its fallback text's UTF-16 length for one written as text (#1099).
  • Unfetchable images. Every fill batchUpdate goes through CellImages.execute, which fill_tables requires, so there's one send path. On an image-fetch error it replaces that image's insert with its fallback text and drops its link, removes it from the URIs, tells _apply_doc_content (which records the error on the image's entry), and resends. An image that never resolved gets its fallback text from the start. The replacement never moves another request: within a cell the images go last, latest first, and cells run latest first. The loop is batch_retry.send_dropping_failed_images, which the body's retry uses too; the two differ only in where they split. As in the body (#510), the first retry resends the whole batch; from the second failure on, the batch splits at the failed image, the requests ahead of it are sent on their own, and only the rest is retried. A batchUpdate applies its requests in order, so sending L[:i] and then L[i:] does what sending L would. A split anywhere else is wrong: sending every cell's text first and the images after (the body's prefix/tail split) moves each later cell's image by the length of every earlier cell's text.
  • Retry bookkeeping. CellImages maps each insert it built to its image and link, holding the request dicts themselves, and clears the map once that batch settles. Keyed on id() alone, a freed insert's key outlived it, and a later batch's insert could be allocated at the same address and pick up the stale link (PR #1215 QA round 1). The body's maps don't need this: content_requests keeps their requests alive.
  • Images the fill never placed. A cell the fill can't locate in the live doc gets no insert, and after a split, the head of a batch lands before the rest can fail for another reason (a 5xx, say). CellImages.embedded grows as each batch lands, the head of a split included, and _apply_doc_content gives every other resolved cell image an error, since it was uploaded and shared and would otherwise read as embedded: after the fill, and on any Exception out of the edit, including a phase-1 failure before the fill starts. A cancellation is left alone: a cancelled execute_in_thread batch still runs to completion, so its images may yet land.

Confirmed live (2026-10-24, two runs): text around an image, an image-only cell, a linked image, an unreachable URL (dropped and reported, rest of the table intact), a local upload (share revoked afterwards), an image on each side of a nested table and one inside it, and Markdown pipe-table cells with one and two images. get_doc_as_markdown reads them back.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Every image a doc edit embeds from a local path or a drive: source is shared anyone:reader before the edit, because the Docs backend fetches inline images anonymously, and that share is revoked once the edit is over. _apply_doc_content (PR #877) and insert_local_images (PR #903) each implemented that sequence themselves, and the copies had drifted. The gaps PR #903's QA found were in exactly the places they differed:

  • #904. _apply_doc_content had no checkpoint between its shielded image gather and its first doc edit. A cancellation held off by the shield was re-delivered at the content batchUpdate's execute_in_thread, which by then had already handed the request to a worker thread. asyncio.to_thread can't stop a running thread, so a call the client had cancelled still edited the doc.
  • #908. Its success-path revoke was shielded with no checkpoint afterward. A cancellation that arrived during the revoke was absorbed: no warning was logged, and the response that would have reported a revoke failure was discarded.
  • #907. When the in-flight edit landed after the cancellation had unwound, the doc cache could hold the pre-edit state. insert_local_images marked the doc dirty on its cancel path, before the orphaned edit committed, so a read in between re-cached the old content. _apply_doc_content's cancel path didn't invalidate at all.
  • #666 (2). write_doc_content uploads a local image into the server's default folder without marking that folder's listing dirty. A resized drive: copy lands next to its original, which no tool marked dirty either. insert_inline_image had the same gap for its resized drive_file_id copy.

docs.title: images.ImageShareLifecycle
docs.text:
One object per doc edit, holding what the cleanup needs: shares (each (outcome_entry, file_id, permission_id) to revoke), outcomes (every image's entry, for the log), and created_file_ids (files the call made, which the log lists separately from the caller's own drive: files).

  • resolve(coros) runs the upload/share coroutines as a gather shielded from cancellation (return_exceptions=True, as before), then marks dirty every folder a result names in created_in.
  • async with edit(): wraps the doc edit:
  • A checkpoint (#904), inside the try whose handler revokes, so a cancellation landing here still revokes and logs.
  • The body runs inside after_abandoned_calls(mark the doc dirty) (#907, below).
  • A finally around the body marks the doc dirty on every exit, success included. Callers no longer do this themselves.
  • A shielded revoke, then a checkpoint (#908), so a cancellation held off by the revoke's shield is raised here and the handler logs it.
  • On any BaseException the handler revokes (at most once) and logs through log_images_after_failed_edit, then re-raises.

_apply_doc_content converts an Exception leaving the async with into DocEditError with the outcome list (#789), after the lifecycle has already revoked and logged. insert_local_images catches its own batchUpdate failure inside the body, as before. The body also runs when there's nothing to embed, so an all-failed call still checkpoints and logs its orphans (PR #903 QA finding 1).

docs.title: 907 suggested exposing execute_in_thread's future so the cancel path could attach a done-callback. That would mean threading the future out of every request an edit makes, including fill_tables and anchor resolution, which issue their own requests several calls deep. Instead, a context-scoped hook: inside with after_abandoned_calls(callback):, execute_in_thread wraps the worker function so that, if the awaiting task gave up on the call while its thread was running, the thread schedules callback on the loop (call_soon_threadsafe) once it returns or raises. Nested requests are covered because the hook travels in a ContextVar, which gathered tasks and worker threads both copy.
docs.text:
The "gave up while running" check is a lock-guarded pair of flags. The worker sets finished in its finally, and the cancel path sets abandoned only if finished isn't set yet. Either the thread finished first, so the cancel path's own invalidation already runs after the commit, or the call was marked abandoned first, so the callback runs after the commit. A completed call, or a cancelled one whose thread never started, never triggers the callback, so the hook adds no cache writes on the normal path.

The same hook covers _replace_doc_content's clear batchUpdate and insert_inline_image's batchUpdate, which have the same orphaned-edit window but no images to share.

docs.title: created_in (#666)
docs.text: Only the call that creates a file knows its folder (downscale_drive_file picks the original's parent, falling back to the default folder). So upload_and_share_image and upload_and_share_local_image tag any result that carries a file_id they created, an orphan included, with created_in (_with_created_in). The caller never has to work out the folder. record_image_outcome doesn't copy the key into the caller-facing outcome. A drive: source's own file_id never gets one, since nothing was created.

docs.title: insert_inline_image's resized copy
docs.text: insert_inline_image shares nothing temporarily (a drive_file_id must already be public), so it doesn't use the lifecycle. Its auto_downscale copy, though, is created and link-shared for good, and two exits used to lose its ID: a cancellation during the downscale or the edit, and a failed batchUpdate, whose {"error"} result omitted resized_file_id. The downscale is now shielded and followed by a checkpoint. A failed edit's result carries resized_file_id, and a cancelled call logs it as a WARNING, the same treatment PR #877 gave temporary shares.

docs.title: 666's first item, a files().get() failing after a successful permissions().create() and losing the permission ID, can't happen any more. Since #511, share_image_file takes webContentLink from the create()/get() call that preceded the share and makes no request after it (test_local_path_uploaded_shared_and_resolved asserts no files().get()). There's nothing left to fix.
A cancellation after the edit finished (PR #1029 QA round 1)
docs.text:
The post-revoke checkpoint raises a cancellation that the revoke's shield held off, even though the edit itself completed. For _replace_doc_content that used to read as a partial write: _failed kept the backup copy of a doc whose new content had fully landed (reproduced live). The lifecycle now sets edit_completed once the edit body exits cleanly. _replace_doc_content builds the lifecycle itself, passes it to _apply_doc_content(lifecycle=...), and on a cancellation with edit_completed set it discards the backup (shielded) and re-raises.

create_doc/create_doc_from_file now mark the target folder dirty right after the Drive create(). They used to do it only after the content step, which a cancellation skipped. The doc is in the folder from the create on, and images uploaded later are marked dirty by resolve(). The create itself (_create_doc_file) runs inside after_abandoned_calls, since a create cancelled in flight still lands after the post-create mark_dirty would have run (QA round 2).

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• A failed or cancelled write_doc_content now marks the doc dirty twice: once in the lifecycle and once in _replace_doc_content's _failed. _failed has to keep its own call, because a doc that was cleared and whose _apply_doc_content raised before the edit phase (during image resolution, say) still changed. A redundant mark_dirty costs one SQLite write.
  • _apply_doc_content now takes the lifespan context (lc) instead of the two services, since the lifecycle needs the doc and folder caches too.

docs.title: Local-File Access Policy
docs.text:
Date: 2026-10-10 · Issue: #796 · Modules: new src/mcp_gee_sweet/local_files.py; server.py; the local-I/O sites under tools/

This doc is the implementation design for the policy approved on #796 (2026-10-04). It doesn't revisit the decision. Where carrying the decision out raised a question it didn't answer, the maintainer settled it on 2026-10-10; see Questions resolved during scoping.

docs.title: The decision, restated
docs.text:
• One setting, LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS=full|roots|off.
  • full: any local path (today's behavior).
  • roots: a path must resolve, symlinks included, under a directory listed in LOCAL_FILE_ROOTS.
  • off: no local file access.
  • Default: full under stdio, off under SSE or streamable HTTP.
  • Every local read and write goes through one shared check.
  • Always blocked, in every mode: the server's own CREDENTIALS_PATH, TOKEN_PATH, SERVICE_ACCOUNT_PATH, and .env.
  • In off mode, local-only tools aren't registered. Tools whose only local I/O is an optional local_path stay registered and return a clear error when it's used.
  • Gmail's attachment read moves off the event loop.
  • Out of scope: remote-safe replacements (binary upload, image bytes, large-result destinations, downloads) and input size limits.

docs.title: What changed since the ticket was filed
docs.text:
Checked against develop at f899708:

  • Gmail's attachment read is already off the loop. PR #928 (#896) moved _read_attachment_bytes inside _compose_raw, which runs _build_raw_message via asyncio.to_thread. The last synchronous local read under tools/ is docs/content.py's _read_doc_source_file (Sky's comment on #796). That one is now this ticket's off-loop item.
  • Streamable HTTP is a third transport (#917). The default rule reads "anything but stdio", not "SSE".
  • Markdown/HTML image sources are a local read the ticket didn't list. create_doc, write_doc_content, create_doc_from_file and update_doc_from_file resolve ![](path) / <img src> through _resolve_image_source, which uploads any local path. The shared check has to cover it.
  • export_file and export_revision don't touch disk. They return bytes in-memory. "Downloads and exports" in the decision means download_file, download_folder and sync_folder.

docs.title: 1. One module: src/mcp_gee_sweet/local_files.py
docs.text:
It's a top-level module beside http_transport.py, not under tools/, because server.py needs it at import time for registration and every tool domain needs it at call time. It owns:

  • LocalFileAccess: a StrEnum with FULL, ROOTS, OFF (a str, Enum until #1212, from when the package supported Python 3.10).
  • POLICY: the process's resolved policy (mode, roots, deny-list), computed once at import.
  • check_read(path) -> Path and check_write(path) -> Path: the one shared check. Each returns the resolved Path to use for the I/O, or raises LocalFileAccessError.
  • LocalFileAccessError(ValueError): a ValueError subclass, so _timed's error-visibility allowlist (decision-tool-error-visibility.md) passes its message to the client unchanged. Sites that report errors as {"error": ...} or as per-item failed entries catch it and use str(e).
  • registers_local_only_tools() -> bool: False in off mode.

It imports the credential paths from auth.py. auth.py imports nothing from tools/ or from this module, so there's no cycle.

docs.title: 2. Resolving the mode at import, and the fail-safe
docs.text:
Tool registration runs at import (register_all(tool) in server.py), before main() parses --transport. off mode decides which tools register, so the mode must be known at import too. ENABLED_TOOLS already solves this by reading sys.argv at import (_parse_enabled_tools). The policy does the same:

  1. Extract _cli_transport(argv) -> str from main() (default "stdio"). main() and the policy resolver both call it, so the two can't disagree.
  2. LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS set: use it. Not set: full if the CLI transport is stdio, else off.
  3. Record whether the mode was explicit or defaulted (POLICY.explicit).

--reload is covered. uvicorn's reload worker is a multiprocessing spawn child, and a spawn child inherits the parent's sys.argv. Confirmed with a scratch script: the child saw --transport sse. So docker-compose.yml's --transport sse --reload resolves to off in the worker that actually serves.

The gap argv can't close. mcp_gee_sweet.server:app is a module-level ASGI object. An operator who points uvicorn at it directly (uvicorn mcp_gee_sweet.server:app) never passes --transport, so argv resolution says stdio and the default would be full on a network-facing server. That launch isn't documented, but nothing stops it, and the decision's default exists precisely for network-facing servers. So, a runtime tripwire:

  • _timed already reads ctx.request_context.request for the access log. It's a Starlette Request under SSE and streamable HTTP, and None under stdio.
  • _timed sets a ContextVar, local_files.request_over_http, for the duration of the call.
  • check_read / check_write refuse every path when POLICY.mode is FULL and not POLICY.explicit and request_over_http.get(), with an error naming LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS. The first such refusal logs one WARNING.

An explicit LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS=full over HTTP is honored, because the operator chose it. The tripwire catches only a stdio default leaking onto an HTTP request. In that misconfigured launch the local-only tools are still registered, but every call they make is refused, so the failure is closed.

docs.title: 3. The check
docs.text:
check_read(path) / check_write(path):
  1. tripwire (§2)
  2. mode OFF   -> refuse
  3. p = Path(os.path.realpath(path))        # relative paths resolve against cwd, as open() does
  4. mode ROOTS -> refuse unless p.is_relative_to(r) for some resolved root r
  5. deny-list  -> refuse if p is a credential file (below)
  6. return p

Check before any stat. Several sites currently call Path(x).is_file() / .exists() first and return "No file found at ...". In roots and off mode, that ordering is an existence oracle for paths outside the roots. The check must run first, and its refusal message must be the same whether or not the path exists. realpath needs no existing target: it resolves the existing prefix, so writes to new files work.

Use the returned path. A site does its I/O on the Path the check returned, not on the caller's string. This narrows the window between check and use, though it doesn't close it (see Known limitations).

Containment is a string test on resolved paths, and it fails closed. On a case-insensitive filesystem (macOS APFS default), realpath keeps the caller's spelling of components that exist. Confirmed: realpath("dir/TOKEN.json") != realpath("dir/token.json") for one file. So a differently-cased path can fail the is_relative_to test for a file that really is inside a root (a false refusal), but it can never pass the test for a file outside one.

What's on the deny-list. The decision's four entries, plus the process-level files the maintainer added on 2026-10-10 (open question 2 below):

Entry Why CREDENTIALS_PATH, TOKEN_PATH, SERVICE_ACCOUNT_PATH the server's own credentials (decision) Path(mcp_gee_sweet.__file__).parent / ".env" runtime config, may hold CREDENTIALS_CONFIG (decision) GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, when set an ADC key file: the same class of secret as SERVICE_ACCOUNT_PATH gcloud's default ADC file: $CLOUDSDK_CONFIG/application_default_credentials.json, else ~/.config/gcloud/… (POSIX) or %APPDATA%\gcloud\… (Windows) ADC's fallback when GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS is unset; a user refresh token CACHE_DB_PATH and its SQLite WAL sidecars (-wal, -shm; cache.py sets journal_mode=WAL). With the default location, the whole mcp-gee-sweet cache directory (Policy.deny_dirs), since only the server writes there. Also the pre-0.9.3 default /tmp/mcp_gee_sweet.db and its sidecars, which stay on disk (GHSA-8jqx-w7j8-6xwm) reading exposes cached Drive/Sheets/Docs data; overwriting corrupts the cache LOG_FILE, ACCESS_LOG_FILE, when set a download could overwrite or truncate them (plain FileHandler, no rotated copies to cover)

Entries are included whether or not the file exists yet; an unset optional entry is skipped.

The deny-list compares file identity, not strings. For the same reason, a string compare would let TOKEN.json through on macOS. A hardlink to the token would also slip past it, inside a root or not. At import, resolve each deny-listed path with realpath. Relative defaults like token.json resolve against the startup cwd, which is what auth.py reads. Then a target is refused if:

  • it exists and os.path.samefile(p, entry) holds for an entry that exists (this catches case variants, hardlinks and bind mounts), or
  • it doesn't exist and its realpath equals an entry's realpath under os.path.normcase and casefold(). This is the write case. A download to a TOKEN_PATH that hasn't been written yet would otherwise plant a token the server then loads.

The deny-list applies in full mode too. There it guards a local user against an LLM-composed send_message(attachments=[{local_path: "token.json"}]) or a sync_folder run over the config directory, not against a hostile caller.

Refusal messages name the setting. The only configured values they carry are the roots, so a caller can pick a valid path on the next try (§9):

  • off: "local file access is disabled on this server (LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS=off)"
  • roots: "<path> is outside this server's LOCAL_FILE_ROOTS. Allowed directories: <root>, <root>". Each root is listed by its configured spelling, the one the containment test matches (§3).
  • deny-list: "<path> is one of this server's own credential, config, cache, or log files and can't be read or written by a tool"
  • tripwire: "local file access is disabled for HTTP requests unless LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS is set explicitly"

Don't interpolate TOKEN_PATH's value or other secret-named values into log lines (CodeQL py/clear-text-logging-sensitive-data; see root CLAUDE.md). Echoing the caller's own path back is fine.

docs.title: 4. Configuration validation
docs.text:
Done at import, alongside ENABLED_TOOLS. An invalid value raises SystemExit with a one-line message, so a misconfigured server never starts serving (as implemented, the exit moved to main()'s serving path; see As implemented):

  • LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS not in full|roots|off (case-insensitive).
  • roots with LOCAL_FILE_ROOTS empty or unset.
  • A LOCAL_FILE_ROOTS entry that doesn't exist or isn't a directory.
  • LOCAL_FILE_ROOTS set while the mode isn't roots: log a WARNING that it's ignored, but don't exit.

LOCAL_FILE_ROOTS is split on os.pathsep (: on POSIX, ; on Windows), like PATH/PYTHONPATH, rather than on the comma ENABLED_TOOLS uses: tool names can't contain commas, but paths can. Each root is resolved with realpath once, at import.

docs.title: 5. Site inventory and choke points
docs.text:
Each local read or write gets exactly one check, placed at the narrowest shared function. Function names are given rather than line numbers, since line numbers move.

Tool(s) Local I/O Check site Op upload_local_file, upload_local_folder (per file), insert_local_images and Markdown/HTML local images (via upload_and_share_local_image) open + MediaFileUpload transfer._upload_local_file, at the top read insert_local_images, Markdown/HTML local images stat, image header read, resize read (check_image_file, prepare_local_image) before the upload images.upload_and_share_local_image, at the top, before prepare_local_image. Also replace insert_local_images's own Path(local_path).is_file() pre-check and content._resolve_image_source's with the check (ordering rule, §3) read upload_local_folder iterdir of the folder the folder itself, in the tool, before is_dir() read create_doc_from_file, update_doc_from_file read_text content._read_doc_source_file, at the top, before exists() read import_csv_to_sheet open the tool, before path.open read send_message, create_draft (attachments) read_bytes gmail._read_attachment_bytes (already in a worker thread; the ValueError propagates out of _compose_raw as today's missing-field error does) read download_file _write_atomically, mkdir the tool, before response_limits.validate_local_destination (that helper stats parents) write download_folder, sync_folder (downloads) mkdir, _write_atomically per file the destination root in the tool, before mkdir, plus each file (§6) write sync_folder (uploads, use_checksum hashing, stat) MediaFileUpload, _local_md5, stat each local entry where _sync_level builds local_map / local_folder_map (§6) read sync_folder, upload_local_folder, download_folder: the local_path root mkdir / iterdir the tool, at entry read for upload-only, write for any direction that can download 9 tools with the response-cap bypass (get_sheet_data, get_multiple_sheet_data, get_multiple_spreadsheet_summary, find_in_spreadsheet, get_doc_content, find_in_doc, get_doc_as_markdown, get_message, get_thread) and sync_folder(result_local_path=) mkdir, _write_atomically response_limits.write_capped_result_to_disk, at the top, before validate_local_destination. Check the final dest after the directory join too, since default_filename changes the target. For result_local_path, also sync_folder's own early validate_local_destination(result_local_path, ...), which runs before any transfer and before local_path's mkdir (#990) write

sync_folder's existing "result_local_path inside local_path" ValueError stays as it is and runs after the policy check. The two are independent.

docs.title: 6. Folder walks: check each entry, not just the root
docs.text:
iterdir() followed by is_file() / is_dir() follows symlinks. A symlink inside an allowed root that points at /etc or at the token file is uploaded today, and a pre-existing symlink in a download destination is written through (_write_atomically deliberately writes through a symlinked dest). Checking only the root would miss both, so:

  • Local reads during a walk. _sync_level runs check_read on each p as it builds local_map. A refused file follows the unsafe_names precedent beside it: it doesn't enter local_map, and it surfaces as one local_read_fail step carrying the refusal reason, so dry_run previews it and a real run reports it in failed. That needs no new plan-action kind. local_folder_map gets the same treatment for symlinked subdirectories, so recursion never descends outside a root. upload_local_folder's per-file _upload_local_file call already gets its check from §5; a refusal lands in failed like any other per-file error.
  • Local writes during a walk. Every _write_atomically call site in download_folder and _sync_level's download branch runs check_write(dest_file) before streaming. A refusal goes to failed. Don't put the check inside _write_atomically: its callers already handle per-file errors differently, and the error should be reported before the Drive download starts, not after.
  • Drive-supplied names can't escape the destination root on their own (_safe_local_dest / _unsafe_name_reason). The per-file check is for symlinks and the deny-list, not for traversal.

A refused entry never aborts the whole walk. That matches how every other per-file failure in these tools is reported.

docs.title: 7. Registration in off mode
docs.text:
Add a local_only: bool = False keyword to server.tool(). Mark the tools at their own decorator (@tool(local_only=True)), not in a central list of names, because a renamed tool silently drops out of a central list. That's the failure gen_tool_docs.py's SUBSETS check exists to catch.

tool() skips registration when local_only and not local_files.registers_local_only_tools(), the same way it skips a tool missing from ENABLED_TOOLS. If ENABLED_TOOLS names a tool that off mode drops, log one WARNING at startup listing the dropped names, so an operator who asked for sync_folder learns why it's missing.

Nine tools are local-only: the decision's seven (sync_folder, upload_local_file, upload_local_folder, download_folder, insert_local_images, create_doc_from_file, update_doc_from_file), plus download_file and import_csv_to_sheet, which take a required local_path and were added by the maintainer on 2026-10-10 (open question 1 below).

Every other tool with local I/O stays registered and reaches the check at call time:

  • the nine response-cap local_path tools
  • send_message / create_draft (attachments[].local_path; content_base64 still works in off mode)
  • create_doc / write_doc_content (local image sources fail per image through the existing image-outcome path, and the doc is still written)

Each local-only tool's docstring gains one sentence, "Not available when the server runs with LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS=off.", so docs/tools.md (generated) says so too.

docs.title: 8. Off-loop read
docs.text: _read_doc_source_file keeps its signature. Both callers wrap it as await asyncio.to_thread(_read_doc_source_file, ...). The policy check runs inside it, at the top, so it runs on the worker thread with the read. Nothing else under tools/ reads file contents on the loop (grep -rn "read_text\|read_bytes" src/mcp_gee_sweet/tools). The cheap stat calls that remain on the loop (the check's realpath/samefile, is_dir()) are in the same cost class as the is_file() pre-checks that already run there, so they don't move.

docs.title: 9. Reporting the policy to callers
docs.text:
A model working in roots mode otherwise has to guess paths until one passes. The MCP reference filesystem server addresses the same problem with a list_allowed_directories tool. Here the information goes in two places that already exist, so no new tool is added:

  • The roots refusal message lists the allowed directories (§3). It reaches the model exactly when it hits the boundary, including in clients that never surface resources.
  • server://auth-status gains a top-level local_file_access object, set identically in all three of _auth_status_json's return branches (unauthorized, service account, full access):
"local_file_access": {
  "mode": "roots",
  "explicit": true,
  "roots": ["/data", "/srv/exports"],
  "unregistered_tools": []
}
  • mode: the resolved mode.
  • explicit: whether LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS was set (§2). A defaulted full over HTTP is refused per call by the tripwire. The resource is static and can't see the reading request's transport, so explicit: false with mode: "full" is the signal a client gets.
  • roots: the configured roots in roots mode; an empty list otherwise.
  • unregistered_tools: in off mode, the local-only tools this policy kept from registering, i.e. those ENABLED_TOOLS would otherwise have allowed. Empty otherwise. This is separate from limited_tools/limitations, which describe registered tools that fail for auth reasons.

The resource's docstring gains a sentence describing the field.

Publishing the roots discloses directory paths, which can hint at the host's layout, but only paths the caller is already allowed to read and write. There's no setting to hide them. One can be added if an operator asks.

docs.title: 10. Docs and release notes
docs.text:
• docs/configuration.md: LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS and LOCAL_FILE_ROOTS in the environment-variable table, plus a short section with the transport defaults, the always-blocked list, and a Docker bind-mount example (LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS=roots, LOCAL_FILE_ROOTS=/data).
  • src/mcp_gee_sweet/.env.template: both settings, commented out.
  • CHANGELOG.md: a Breaking entry. An SSE or streamable-HTTP server that relied on local-path tools must now set LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS.
  • docs/known-limitations.md: the limitations below.
  • Root CLAUDE.md: a one-paragraph invariant entry ("every local read/write goes through local_files.check_read/check_write; local-only tools take @tool(local_only=True)"), since a future tool that forgets the check is the regression this design is most exposed to.
  • docker-compose.yml needs no change. It mounts no data directory, so off is the right default for it, and its service-account key is deny-listed anyway.

docs.title: 11. Tests
docs.text:
Unit tests only for the policy itself; it has no Google API surface.

  • tests/test_local_files.py:
  • The mode matrix: LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS unset/each value × --transport absent/stdio/sse/streamable-http.
  • Validation exits (§4).
  • roots containment with tmp_path: inside, outside, .. traversal, a symlink inside a root pointing outside, a symlink outside pointing inside.
  • The deny-list: a case variant (skip unless the filesystem is case-insensitive), a hardlink, a non-existent TOKEN_PATH as a write target, .env, the cache's -wal sidecar, CLOUDSDK_CONFIG overriding the ADC default, an unset LOG_FILE adding no entry.
  • The tripwire: defaulted full + HTTP request refuses; explicit full + HTTP request allows; stdio allows.
  • Identical refusal text for existing vs. missing paths outside a root, listing the configured roots.
  • tests/test_server.py, server://auth-status: local_file_access is present in all three _auth_status_json branches, with roots filled only in roots mode and unregistered_tools only in off mode (and narrowed by ENABLED_TOOLS). Extend TestResourcesReadLifespanContext's pattern; docs/qa/tests/infra.md gets a TC next to TC-I27 for a live resource read.
  • tests/test_server.py: in off mode the nine tools aren't registered and the rest are; the ENABLED_TOOLS warning. Follow the existing ENABLED_TOOLS tests' monkeypatch of sys.argv and the module attribute rather than re-importing server.
  • One test per §5 choke point: in off mode the tool returns the refusal and the filesystem is untouched (no file created, no mkdir, no Drive call made).
  • sync_folder / upload_local_folder / download_folder: a walked directory with one symlink escaping the root. The other files transfer, and the escaping one is a failed / local_read_fail entry, under dry_run as well.
  • A guard test: every @tool function with a parameter named local_path or result_local_path, or attachments/images, appears in an explicit allowlist of tools whose checks are covered above. A new local-path tool then fails CI until someone decides where its check goes.

Live QA: the policy makes no Google API calls of its own, so live QA is limited to confirming the real launch paths. One stdio and one SSE subprocess run through tests/integration/ (decision-local-fs-test-harness.md): under SSE with no setting, sync_folder is absent from tools/list; with LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS=roots, upload_local_file works inside the root and is refused outside it.

docs.title: As implemented
docs.text:
Where the implementation goes beyond the design above:

  • The off refusal says why when the mode was defaulted. An explicit off reads as in §3. A defaulted one reads local file access is disabled on this server: LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS is unset, which means off for the <transport> transport, since (LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS=off) would name a setting the operator never made. The deny-list message ends can't be read by a tool or can't be written by a tool, depending on the operation.
  • An optional local_path is also checked at the tool's entry. A live SSE run showed get_sheet_data(local_path=...) in off mode fetching first: a bad spreadsheet ID reported its 404 instead of the refusal, and a good one paid for a fetch it would then refuse to write. The ten tools with an optional local_path now call check_write before any API call. write_capped_result_to_disk keeps its own check as the backstop.
  • sync_folder checks a download's target even when nothing exists locally. §6 checks each local entry; a Drive-only file is checked at the path it would be written to, so a Drive file named token.json can't plant a token in the directory holding TOKEN_PATH. A name on one side only that the direction never touches (local-only under download, Drive-only under upload) is planned as the usual skip without a check (_sync_policy_refusal), the way _unsafe_name_step treats an unsafe name.
  • The docstring note joins each local-only tool's first paragraph. gen_tool_docs.py takes only the first paragraph, so a separate one wouldn't have reached docs/tools.md.
  • An invalid setting doesn't exit at import (PR #1039 QA round 1, finding 4). §4's import-time SystemExit also blocked mcp-gee-sweet auth and gen_tool_docs.py, neither of which serves, and a roots entry that isn't mounted yet blocked re-authorization. resolve_policy now resolves an invalid setting to off, the fail-safe for registration, with the reason in Policy.error. It logs one ERROR at import, and main()'s serving path exits on it with the same one-line message (exit_if_invalid).
  • sync_folder's verb follows the operation (finding 3). _sync_local_check maps (in_drive, in_local, direction) to no check, check_read, check_write, or check_read_write for a both-sides entry under bidirectional, whose refusal says "can't be read or written". The sync root counts as a both-sides entry, and _unsafe_name_step's skip rule uses the same helper.
  • A NUL byte is a refusal, not a crash (finding 1). os.path.realpath raises a plain ValueError for one, which the per-item sites didn't catch; _check turns it into a LocalFileAccessError, so that item fails alone, as a missing file did before.
  • The case-insensitive compare applies only to a target that doesn't exist (finding 5). An existing target matches by exact path or file identity, so on a case-sensitive filesystem a distinct Token.json beside token.json is allowed.
  • many_checks() for walks (finding 6). A check cost about 75µs, most of it realpath's lstat per component plus a stat of every deny-list entry. Inside many_checks(), which wraps the walks in upload_local_folder, download_folder and sync_folder, the deny-list is statted once and each parent directory resolved once, leaving one lstat per entry: about 13µs. The parent cache is keyed by the path's raw spelling and never normalizes lexically (QA round 2): os.path.abspath collapsed <symlink>/.. before the symlink was resolved, so a walk rooted there checked one directory and wrote into another. A relative path bypasses the cache.
  • No CHANGELOG entry. CHANGELOG.md stops at 0.8.1, so the breaking default for network transports goes in the PR body for the release notes instead.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Check-then-use race. A symlink swapped between the check and the open defeats roots. A remote caller can't create symlinks through any tool (downloads write regular files and sync_folder never creates links), so exploiting it needs a local actor with write access inside a root. Closing it fully would mean openat-style descriptor-relative I/O through every site, which is out of proportion here.
  • roots false refusals on case-insensitive filesystems when the caller's spelling of a directory differs from the root's (§3). This fails closed. Callers should use the root's spelling.
  • Deny-list scope. Only the server's own files (§3's table) are protected. Another secret inside an allowed root, or anywhere in full mode, is readable by design. roots is the tool for limiting that.

docs.title: Questions resolved during scoping
docs.text:
These came out of carrying the decision through. The maintainer answered all three on 2026-10-10.

  1. ~~download_file and import_csv_to_sheet in off mode.~~ Resolved 2026-10-10: unregistered. Each takes a required local_path, so registered it could only ever return the refusal. Folded into §7.
  2. ~~More deny-list candidates.~~ Resolved 2026-10-10: all added. GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, gcloud's default ADC file, CACHE_DB_PATH (with its WAL sidecars), LOG_FILE, ACCESS_LOG_FILE. Folded into §3.
  3. ~~Telling callers about the policy.~~ Resolved 2026-10-10: report it. The mode is always shown in server://auth-status, and in roots mode the roots are shown both there and in the refusal message. No hide setting. See §9.

docs.title: Design: CommonMark/GFM Markdown Parser
docs.text: Status: Implemented in #1116 (closes #1071 too). Replaces the Python-Markdown call in markdown-support.md; the MD → HTML → AST → Docs pipeline that doc describes is unchanged. Also answers #1112's open questions (Joy's spike, closed into #1116).

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: _md_to_html parsed with Python-Markdown, which departs from CommonMark/GFM, the dialect models and most tools write: a list or table directly under a paragraph stayed text, 1) wasn't a list, \-escapes kept their backslash, bold inside italic was lost, sub-lists needed 4 spaces, fenced code inside a list item was literal text, ~~ did nothing. The #1044 Phase 2 baseline (docs/qa/results/2026-10-18-markdown-phase2.md) found each one live. The maintainer decision (2026-10-18) was to replace the parser rather than patch Python-Markdown's grammar case by case.
