docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
src/mcp_gee_sweet/tools/docs/md_to_html.py, imported by content.py:

_md_to_html(md, autolink_urls)
  = markdown-it("commonmark", html=True) + table + strikethrough
      .render(_preprocess(normalize_line_endings(md)))
Piece Why markdown-it-py, commonmark preset CommonMark-conformant, already in the lock as a transitive dependency (now a direct one). html=True keeps raw HTML passing through to html_to_ast, as before. table, strikethrough rules GFM's two block/inline extensions. Task lists are left as literal [ ]/[x] text, which html_to_ast already turns into checkbox items, so no plugin is needed. _gfm_autolink_rule (core rule) GFM extended autolinks: www., http(s)://, email. See below. normalizeLink = identity markdown-it percent-encodes destinations; a local image path like café.png would no longer open. validateLink still refuses javascript: and friends. _spaced_image_rule, _spaced_link_rule (inline rules) ![alt](/path/Screen Shot.png), [notes](./My Notes.md "t"): Python-Markdown accepted a space in a link or image destination, CommonMark doesn't, and existing .md files rely on it. Only that shape is taken: two or more space-separated pieces with no quotes, parens or angle brackets, then an optional quoted title. Anything CommonMark itself parses as a link or image never reaches them. The destination is unescaped like any other (\_, &) and refused if that yields a quote; the match stops at posMax (a link label's end, inside one); a label naming a reference definition stays that reference; and no link opens inside another's label. maxNesting = 100 The commonmark preset's 20 silently dropped everything deeper, and each list level costs two (ul + li), so an item's text vanished from about level 10. Python-Markdown kept it. 100 keeps 50 list levels and still parses ">" * 1200. _preprocess (one line-based pre-pass) Plan rules D1 and D2. See below. asyncio.to_thread in _apply_doc_content The parse is pure CPU, about 2× Python-Markdown's time on realistic input (0.2 s for 50 KB) and up to 5× on emphasis-heavy input, all linear. It ran on the event loop before too; now the Markdown step doesn't. Ruler caches built at import Both renderers and the block scanner are shared by every to_thread worker, and markdown-it builds a ruler's rule cache lazily on first use. Every ruler's cache is built at import, so concurrent first conversions never see a half-built one.

Each conversion block-parses the document twice: once in _preprocess (_verbatim_lines, inline pass off) and once to render.

markdown (Python-Markdown) stays a dependency: anchors.py uses its toc slugify for the GitLab heading-anchor scheme. upload_file(source_format='markdown') (EP-8) renders with this converter since #1102: with convert_to_doc=True through create_doc's whole path, and without it as the uploaded HTML file.

docs.title: Autolinks: a GFM rule, not linkify-it
docs.text:
markdown-it's own linkify needs linkify-it-py and doesn't follow GFM. Measured: with fuzzy links on, it links README.md, file.py and example.com (any TLD-looking token); with them off, it stops linking www. too; it also links ftp://. The GFM rule is short, so it's a core rule over text tokens instead:

  • www. or http(s):// plus a domain, or an email address, after whitespace, *, _, ~ or (. A text token's own start counts only at the start of the inline content, after a line break, or after an emphasis or strikethrough delimiter (_AUTOLINK_BOUNDARY_TOKENS). So, as in GFM, a URL right after a code span, a link, an inline tag (<b>https://x.com</b>) or a character like : (URL:https://x.com) isn't linked. The Python-Markdown-era bare-URL extension linked those last two; CHANGELOG.md says so.
  • No _ in the last two domain segments, and no empty segment. A scheme-ful link may have a one-segment domain (http://localhost:8000), as in cmark-gfm.
  • Trailing ?!.,:*_~'", an unbalanced ), and a trailing &entity; are left outside the link. The domain is checked after that trim, since it can eat the domain (http://__, www.__ aren't links), and a link is scheme-ful only if it starts with http:// or https:// (so www.x.com/a://b still gets a scheme added).
  • A www. link gets https://, not GFM's http:// (#1281): emitter._storable_link_url gives a written scheme-less www. target https:// (#1180), and one host shouldn't get both schemes in one doc.
  • Runs after inline parsing, so a code span, an <autolink> or raw HTML is never re-matched; text inside a Markdown link or a raw-HTML <a> is skipped, since links can't nest.
  • Linear in the text: emails are found outwards from each @ (_gfm_email_matches), and _trim_autolink works back from the end with running paren counts. See "Review history".

autolink_urls=False drops the rule, so www., email and https:// are all plain text.

docs.title: _preprocess: plan rules D1 and D2
docs.text:
One pass over the lines, keeping a stack of open list items (_ListItemColumns: original and rewritten marker and content columns). It keeps the line count, except for D2's inserted blank lines, which _rewrite returns as lines with no source index so a quote run can put its prefixes back.

Code and raw HTML are never read as Markdown. _verbatim_lines runs markdown-it's own block parser (inline pass off) once, and returns every line of an indented code block or raw HTML block and the body and closing fence of a fenced block, mapped to the block's first line. A fence opened on a marker line (- ```) or inside a quote is found the way the renderer finds it. Those lines are only moved with the item they belong to (a fence body by its opening line's shift), and only their item's own indentation is rewritten (_shift_verbatim): whitespace past the item's content column is the code's, tabs included, so a Makefile recipe keeps its tab.

D1: nesting width (#1071). Plan rule D1 (docs/qa/tests/docs_markdown.md): a marker indented at least 2 columns past the previous item's marker nests under it, whatever the parent marker's width. CommonMark nests only at the parent's content column, so 1. A / - a (column 2 < 3) doesn't nest, and under markdown-it the grandchildren of a 2-space numbered outline became literal 1. Grandchild text. For each marker line:

  • pop items until the top's marker is at least 2 columns left of this one; an item within 0–1 columns is a sibling, and the line moves as far as that sibling moved, not onto its column;
  • under a parent, the marker moves to the parent's rewritten content column, plus however far past the original content column it already was, so 4-space and tab indents are unchanged;
  • continuation lines move by their owning item's shift.

Right under paragraph text (a list item's own text counts), a marker opens a new list only if CommonMark lets it interrupt a paragraph: a bullet or 1./1) with text after it. Otherwise (Some text / 2019. A great year) it is paragraph text. One exception: a child candidate short of its parent's content column isn't inside the parent's paragraph at all, so CommonMark reads it at the parent's own level (1. A / 2. b is two items), and so does the pass.

A tab after a moved marker is written as the spaces it spanned (_moved_marker_line): moved, the same tab would reach a different tab stop and change the item's content column. Tab widths after a marker count from the marker's column (_space_after_marker), and leading columns count tabs to the next multiple of 4, as CommonMark does.

A run of quoted lines not indented into a list ends any open list and gets the same rules one level in: each line's > prefix is stripped, the inner lines go through _rewrite with the verbatim map sliced to them by bisect (no second parse, no scan of the whole map), and the prefixes are put back, so > 1. A / > - a nests. Past _MAX_QUOTE_DEPTH (markdown-it's maxNesting, 100) quotes are left as written. A quote inside a list item isn't rewritten, and neither is anything after a list ends (a blank line then unindented text, or a heading, quote, fence or thematic break). A lazy line starting with | that isn't a table is paragraph text and doesn't end the list.

D2: a table starts its own block. GFM lets a table interrupt a paragraph, but not a list item's or a quote's lazy continuation, so - B / | K | V | / |---|---| made the rows more item text. A blank line goes in before a table header only where it would be read that way: right under a list item's text (or lazy text continuing it) or a quote run, and not indented into the item. A table indented into an item already renders inside it, and one under a plain paragraph already renders as a table; a blank line there would only make a list loose (and html_to_ast then drops its bullets, #1111). A header needs a delimiter row with a | and the same number of cells, so a setext underline (a | b / ---) isn't split from its heading text. Inside a quote, the inserted line is a bare >, so the table stays in the quote. A table indented into an item right after a quote in that item (- a / > q / | x |) would be the quote's lazy text, and a blank line would make the list loose; an HTML comment line (_LAZY_BREAK, which html_to_ast ignores) ends the quote instead and keeps the table in the item. Two tables with no blank line between stay one table (AJ-078: GFM ends a table only at a blank line or another block).

Where this departs from CommonMark. Running all 652 CommonMark spec examples through _md_to_html and plain markdown-it (same rules, raw destinations) differs in exactly four, all by design: example 297 (10) foo / - bar: the bullet nests), 311 and 313 (1. a, blank, 2. b: 2. nests under 1., where CommonMark has siblings or, in 313, a code block), and 488 ([link](/my uri) is a link, _spaced_link_rule).

docs.title: The HTML html_to_ast sees
docs.text:
Inventory of where markdown-it's HTML differs from Python-Markdown's, and what handles it:

Shape Python-Markdown markdown-it Handling Tight item with a nested block <li>a<ul> <li>a <ul> (also before <pre>, <table>, <blockquote>) Changed: _interrupt_open_block drops trailing whitespace holding a line break from the raw text before the block. It was reaching the Docs API as an empty paragraph under every parent item. A <br>'s own break is kept. Rule inside an item (never produced) <li>item <hr /> </li> Changed: an <hr> after text in an open block, or in a resumed segment (after a nested list or quote in the item), ends that segment, emits the rule's empty paragraph, and resumes the block. <li><hr> with no text is an empty bullet with the rule inside the item (#1075). Text after a block in an item (never produced) <hr /> more</li> Changed: a resumed segment drops the line break at its start, as the break before a block is dropped. An authored   there isn't ASCII whitespace and stays (#444). Loose item <li> <p>a</p> </li> same Unchanged here: handled by community PR #1164 (#1111), merged into develop before this PR. markdown-it produces it more often, since it attaches an indented paragraph or code block to the item instead of dropping it out of the list. Strikethrough (none) <s> Already handled (_INLINE_STRIKE). Table alignment align="left" style="text-align:left" Neither is read; no AST field for column alignment. No regression. Code block language class="language-x" same Unchanged. Hard break <br /> same Unchanged; the double break it produces is #1117. Now reachable from a trailing \ too. Two quotes one <blockquote>, two <p> two <blockquote> Renders as two quotes (#1098's emitter work). Empty item (not produced) <li></li> An empty bullet (#1075). Output no trailing newline ends in Harmless; one exact-match test updated.

docs.title: Behavior changes for existing callers
docs.text:
Measured by rendering every fixture under docs/qa/fixtures/md/ through both parsers into the AST and diffing (32 of 52 fixtures changed). Each change is one of the fixes in #1116's table, D1, D2, or listed here; CHANGELOG.md has the user-facing version.

  • Fixed: everything in #1116's table; 2-, 3- and 4-space nesting (TC-MD106 LN-01 to LN-16 all match their expectation on screen; r16's agenda is one list numbered 1–4 in the HTML and the AST, but on screen Docs still restarts it at 1 after each sub-list, which is the emitter's #1072, live in TC-MD016); blocks inside list items (TC-MD201); fenced code inside items renders as code without the info string as text; strikethrough; www/email autolinks; \ escapes; adjacent quotes; a bare - no longer becomes a setext heading.
  • Loose lists, with #1164 in: in CommonMark one blank line anywhere in a list (- a, - b, blank, - c) makes the whole list loose (<li><p>), and so does an item with an indented paragraph or code block under it (r06's numbered steps, TC-MD107, TC-MD108 LX-08, TC-MD203's list-after-list pairs, which CommonMark merges into one loose list). Without #1164 every such item lost its bullet (#1111); with it, which this branch merged before approval, every one keeps its bullet. Python-Markdown kept some of those items bulleted, or dropped the blocks out of the list and restarted the numbering. A block inside a numbered item now stays inside one <ol>, so the AST keeps every item ordered. At the switch, the emitter still split the list around the block and Docs restarted the numbering on screen; #1094 later fixed that (see "Fixed after the switch" below).
  • A setext underline under an item's text (- a / ---) makes that text a Heading 2 inside the item, as CommonMark reads it; Python-Markdown kept the item and a rule. At the switch the heading lost its bullet in the AST; #1094 later made the item a bulleted Heading 2. *** is a rule in either parser.
  • Different, still wrong: front matter (DS-14) renders as a rule plus a Heading 2 instead of a rule, a paragraph and a rule (#1173).
  • Fixed after the switch (#1094): a block inside a list item rendered after the item, at the margin, since the AST had no way to put a block inside an item, and the next item restarted the numbering. The block now carries its item's list_depth: it's indented under the item and the list continues past it.
  • Unchanged: r03, r07, code blocks, inline code, inline HTML, images, unicode, and DS-01 to DS-13 (CRLF included).

docs.title: Re-run scope
docs.text:
Every Markdown entry point that uses _md_to_html (EP-1 to EP-4). EP-5 to EP-7 (Drive's native import) and EP-8 don't use it.

  • The #1116 table: TC-MD202, TC-MD108 (LX-01, LX-02), TC-MD113 (TB-04, TB-08), TC-MD105 (LM-03), TC-MD114 (BR-03), TC-MD101 (HD-02, HD-04), TC-MD115 (ES-01), TC-MD102 (EM-04), TC-MD204 (IN-05), TC-MD111 (LK-06, LK-07).
  • D1 (#1071): TC-MD106, TC-MD109 (TK-02), TC-MD016, TC-MD001, TC-MD002, TC-MD012.
  • Changed fixtures, for regressions: TC-MD004–TC-MD006, TC-MD008–TC-MD011, TC-MD013–TC-MD015, TC-MD107, TC-MD110, TC-MD201, TC-MD203, TC-MD301 (DS-14), TC-MD302.
  • The rest of docs_markdown.md produced the same AST and needs no re-run for this change.

docs.title: What this does NOT do
docs.text:
• Strip front matter (#1173), keep an empty list item (#1075), keep a loose item's bullet (#1164, already in develop), or fix hard and soft breaks (#1117, #1093). Each is in the HTML → AST step or its own ticket.
  • Change EP-8 (upload_file), which kept Python-Markdown until #1102.
  • Read table column alignment.

docs.title: Review history
docs.text:
PR #1228's QA rounds, and what each changed. The invariants they produced are in CLAUDE.md's docs/md_to_html.py entry.

  • Round 1 (8 findings). The two pre-passes tracked fences by hand, so they missed a fence opened on a list-marker line and every raw HTML block, and rewrote code inside them. Replaced by _verbatim_lines, from markdown-it's own block parser. Also: the pass ignored CommonMark's paragraph-interrupt rule (2019. A great year opened a list); a bare --- counted as a delimiter row, splitting a setext heading; the email regex was quadratic on _-heavy text ("a_" * 20000 took about a second), replaced by the scan out from each @; text after a code span or link was autolinked; the spaced-image rule didn't unescape or respect posMax; tab widths after a marker counted from column 0. A run of the CommonMark spec examples then found siblings snapping onto their sibling's rewritten column (example 310).
  • Round 2 (9 findings). D2's blank line went in before a table already indented into an item, which made the list loose and lost its bullets: D2 moved into the D1 pass, which knows which item a line belongs to, and the separate table pass (and its second block parse) went away. Also: _trim_autolink was quadratic on a run of entities or parens; the quote recursion had no depth cap (">" * 1200 raised RecursionError) and parsed again per quote run; the shared parsers' ruler caches were built lazily, racing across to_thread workers; _md_to_html(x, None) raised KeyError; and the html_parser trim before a block removed a <br>'s break, now marked _LineBreak so only source text is trimmed. The stricter GFM link boundary (URL:https://x.com, <b>https://x.com</b> not linked) was kept and documented.
  • Round 3 (10 findings, plus the live matrix). The branch had fallen behind develop, so CI hadn't run; merged. In html_parser, a rule after a nested list in an item took the dropped-construct path and left the resumed segment's \ns as empty bullets, and text after a rule kept a leading break: a resumed segment now takes the <hr> interrupt path and drops a leading line break. In the pre-pass: each quote run scanned the whole verbatim map (now a bisect slice); moving an item rebuilt a fence body's whole indentation, turning a recipe tab into spaces (_shift_verbatim keeps the code's own whitespace); maxNesting 20 dropped deep list text (now 100, with _MAX_QUOTE_DEPTH matching); a lazy | line ended the list; and a table after a quote inside an item stayed the quote's lazy text (_LAZY_BREAK). Spaced destinations now take a title, and links get the same rule as images, since existing .md files lose [notes](./My Notes.md) otherwise; the CommonMark spec run caught two edges of that rule (examples 41 and 568). The "r16 keeps 1–4" claim was the HTML's, not the screen's.
  • Round 4 (6 findings). The loose-list regression is wider than round 1's wording said: one blank line anywhere makes a CommonMark list loose, and every item then loses its bullet until #1164; the PR now waits for #1164 (QA won't approve without it). The autolink domain was checked before trimming (http://__ linked an empty host) and the scheme by "://" in label; the resumed-segment trim lacked the <pre> guard its counterpart has; a setext underline under item text is documented as a behavior change; and a stale dev-group markdown-it-py pin was removed.
  • Round 5 (the develop merge). #1164 merged, and develop was merged in: loose lists keep their bullets, and a code block or paragraph inside a numbered item keeps one <ol> (TestLooseListsAfter1164).

docs.title: Design: Markdown Support for Google Docs Tools
docs.text:
Status: Shipped. content_format='markdown' on create_doc/write_doc_content, plus create_doc_from_file, landed via #102/#103/#104 (PR #105); bare-URL autolinking (autolink_urls) landed separately via #248 (PR #265). Live-verified: 2026-06-28 QA results, 2026-07-04 QA results.

Parser superseded (#1116): the Python-Markdown call below was replaced with markdown-it-py (CommonMark plus GFM) in docs/md_to_html.py; see markdown-parser.md. The MD → HTML → AST shape this doc argues for is unchanged.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: create_doc and write_doc_content only accept HTML. Users who work primarily with .md files have to convert manually before calling these tools. The project already has the markdown library as a dependency (used in transfer.py) and a clean HTML → AST → Docs API pipeline, but markdown content never flows through that pipeline.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Add a markdown → HTML shim at the docs layer, then expose it in two ways: 1. A content_format parameter on create_doc and write_doc_content 2. A new create_doc_from_file tool for uploading local .md / .html files

This intentionally does not use Drive's native HTML importer (which upload_file did for a Markdown source with convert_to_doc=True until #1102 routed it through this pipeline too). Routing through our AST pipeline gives consistent formatting control and benefits from all the Phase 2 work (correct heading levels, colspan, header cells, column widths, etc.).

docs.title: Why MD → HTML → AST (not a direct MD → AST parser)
docs.text:
Markdown is defined by its spec as shorthand for HTML — the spec describes every construct in terms of its HTML output, not in terms of a semantic document model. So markdown the library isn't doing a lossy conversion; it's doing exactly what the format specifies. Chaining it into html_to_ast is two well-tested parsers each doing precisely what they were designed for, not two approximations stacked on top of each other.

A direct MD → AST parser would duplicate all the logic already in html_to_ast (heading detection, inline formatting stacks, list depth tracking, table parsing) — more code, more edge cases, two things to maintain.

The one real exception: constructs that don't survive the HTML round-trip cleanly:

  • Code blocks — <pre><code> carries no semantic signal that our HTML parser acted on until text styles landed, so they used to fall through to plain text.
  • Task list state — - [x] item emits <input type="checkbox" checked> in HTML; the HTML parser ignores raw <input>, so checked/unchecked state had to be captured earlier, at the markdown layer itself.

Resolved by #104: task-list markers are stripped from the item's text and captured on BulletItem.checked, and the emitter prepends a ☑/☐ glyph — not a BULLET_CHECKBOX preset list. Resolved by #103: <pre>/<code> now set font_family="Courier New" on their runs (tracked via html_parser.py's _in_pre/_code_depth), emitted through weightedFontFamily in emitter.py — no separate CodeBlock AST node was needed. The HTML intermediary handled both constructs without needing to become a direct MD → AST parser.

docs.title: File changed
docs.text: Only one file at the time this landed: src/mcp_gee_sweet/tools/docs/__init__.py. The Docs package was later split by domain (#64); this logic now lives in src/mcp_gee_sweet/tools/docs/content.py.

docs.title: 1. New import + helper
docs.text:
import markdown as _md  # already a dep; add import at top of docs/__init__.py


def _md_to_html(md_text: str) -> str:
    return _md.markdown(md_text, extensions=["tables", "fenced_code", "sane_lists"])

Extensions chosen: - tables — GitHub-flavored pipe tables → <table> - fenced_code — triple-backtick blocks → <pre><code> (renders as plain text for now) - sane_lists — correct mixed list handling - nl2br intentionally excluded — single newlines within a paragraph should be ignored (standard Markdown), not become <br> tags

docs.title: 2. Extend _html_to_doc_requests → _to_doc_requests
docs.text:
Replace: 

def _html_to_doc_requests(html_content, start_index=1):
    nodes = html_to_ast(html_content)
    return ast_to_requests(nodes, start_index)

With: 

def _to_doc_requests(content, content_format="html", start_index=1):
    if content_format == "markdown":
        content = _md_to_html(content)
    nodes = html_to_ast(content)
    return ast_to_requests(nodes, start_index)

Update both call sites in create_doc and write_doc_content.

docs.title: 3. create_doc — add content_format param
docs.text:
def create_doc(title, content=None, folder_id=None, content_format="html", ctx=None):

Docstring update:

Content is interpreted as HTML by default. Pass content_format='markdown' to supply GitHub-flavored Markdown instead.

docs.title: 4. write_doc_content — add content_format param
docs.text:
def write_doc_content(doc_id, content, content_format="html", ctx=None):

Same docstring update.

docs.title: 5. New tool: create_doc_from_file
docs.text:
@tool(annotations=ToolAnnotations(title="Create Document from File", destructiveHint=True))
def create_doc_from_file(
    local_path: str,
    title: str | None = None,
    folder_id: str | None = None,
    ctx: Context = None,
) -> dict:
    """
    Create a Google Doc from a local .md or .html file.

    Format is inferred from the file extension (.md → markdown, .html/.htm → HTML).
    Title defaults to the filename without extension.

    Note: same auth constraints as create_doc — requires OAuth or ADC for personal Drive.
    """
    from pathlib import Path

    path = Path(local_path)
    if not path.exists():
        return {"error": f"File not found: {local_path}"}

    ext = path.suffix.lower()
    if ext == ".md":
        content_format = "markdown"
    elif ext in (".html", ".htm"):
        content_format = "html"
    else:
        return {"error": f"Unsupported file extension '{ext}'. Use .md or .html"}

    content = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    doc_title = title or path.stem

    # --- same body as create_doc from here ---
    lc = ctx.request_context.lifespan_context
    drive_service = lc.drive_service
    docs_service = lc.docs_service
    target_folder_id = folder_id or lc.folder_id
    # ... create file, call _to_doc_requests(content, content_format, 1), fill_tables, etc.

The tool body is a copy of create_doc's internals (can't call a registered tool from another registered tool), passing content_format through to _to_doc_requests.

docs.title: Markdown → Docs mapping
docs.text:
Markdown input HTML emitted AST node Google Docs result # Heading 1 <h1> Heading(level=1) HEADING_1 paragraph style **bold** <strong> Run(bold=True) bold text run *italic* <em> Run(italic=True) italic text run ~~strikethrough~~ <s> (GFM strikethrough) Run(strikethrough=True) struck-through text run (#1077) <s>, <strike>, <del> (inline HTML) passed through Run(strikethrough=True) struck-through text run (#1077) <sub>, <sup> (inline HTML) passed through Run(baseline_offset="SUBSCRIPT"/"SUPERSCRIPT"); the innermost open tag wins subscript / superscript text run (#1119) <mark> (inline HTML) passed through Run(background_color= yellow ) yellow-highlighted text run (#1119) [text](url) <a href=...> Run(link_url=...) hyperlink bare https://url <a href=...> (autolink extension) Run(link_url=...) hyperlink — disable via autolink_urls=False [![alt](src)](url) <a href=...><img ...></a> Image(link_url=...) linked inline image (#977) - item <ul><li> BulletItem(ordered=False) disc bullet list 1. item <ol><li> BulletItem(ordered=True) numbered list - [x] item <input type="checkbox" checked> BulletItem(checked=True) bullet with a ☑/☐ glyph prefix a block indented under an item (a second paragraph, code, a quote, a heading, a table, a rule, an image) the block inside the <li> that block's own node with list_depth = the item's depth (#1094) no bullet, indented to the item's text (a quote one step further, with its border); the list continues past it, so the next item keeps its number - # Heading (a heading as the item's own text) <li><h1> BulletItem(heading_level=1) a bulleted HEADING_1 paragraph (#1094) \| a \| b \| <table> Table table via two-phase fill `code` <code> Run(font_family="Courier New") monospace text run ```code block``` <pre><code> Paragraph (all runs font_family="Courier New") monospace paragraph, 8pt above and below (#1098) > quoted text <blockquote><p> Paragraph(blockquote_depth=1) (or Heading/BulletItem/NamedBlock, whichever the quoted content is) left border + indent, scaled by nesting depth (#476), 8pt above and below the quote; adjacent quotes kept apart (#1098) — see blockquote-representation.md

Code blocks and inline code render with font_family="Courier New" on every run (#103) — no further code-block-specific styling (background shading, line numbers) is planned.

A multi-line code block's own internal line breaks are emitted as "\v" (soft break), not "\n" — the Docs API treats a literal "\n" as a new paragraph boundary regardless of styling, which used to fragment one fenced block into one NORMAL_TEXT Docs paragraph per line (#719), contradicting the "monospace paragraph" (singular) mapping above. See CLAUDE.md's docs/emitter.py paragraph for the full fix, including the matching read-side reversal in doc_to_ast.py.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
1. uv run python -m pytest tests/ — no regressions
  2. New unit tests in tests/test_docs.py:
  3. _md_to_html produces expected HTML for headings, bold, lists, tables
  4. _to_doc_requests("# Hello", content_format="markdown") produces the same AST/requests as _to_doc_requests("<h1>Hello</h1>", content_format="html")
  5. Smoke test via create_doc_from_file on a real .md file
  6. Add QA checklist entry to docs/qa/tests/docs.md

docs.title: What this does NOT do
docs.text:
• Does not change upload_file's markdown path (that goes through Drive's native importer, which is fine for raw uploads)
  • Does not support nested tables (a table inside a table cell) via Markdown — the markdown library's table syntax can't express one; see docs/known-limitations.md's Google Docs section for the HTML-input workaround
  • Does not support .md files with front matter (YAML front matter would show up as a <hr> paragraph — acceptable for now). Superseded: plan rule D3 omits it from the Doc through every entry point (#1173, tools/front_matter.py).

docs.title: MCP Bundle (.mcpb)
docs.text:
Issue: #1036. Date: 2026-10-25.

The server ships as an MCP Bundle alongside the PyPI package: a zip holding manifest.json, which tells an MCPB-aware host (Claude Desktop) how to launch the server and what to ask the user for at install.

docs.title: 1036 also meant the bundle for a Smithery listing, which takes a local stdio server only as a .mcpb. That part was dropped: on 2026-10-31 Smithery ends its connection services, deprecates its CLI, and keeps only a non-proxied registry of verified servers' direct MCP URLs (smithery.ai/future), which says nothing about local bundles. The bundle is for one-click installs in an MCPB-aware host.
Pieces
docs.text: File Role manifest.json MCPB manifest v0.4, server.type: "uv". The source of truth for the bundle's metadata and launch command, everything but the version. scripts/build_mcpb.py Stages an allowlist of files as committed at HEAD, stamps the version, and runs mcpb pack (@anthropic-ai/mcpb, pinned). --smoke is the CI check. .mcpbignore A backstop inside the staging directory, not the main guard (below). src/mcp_gee_sweet/__main__.py python -m mcp_gee_sweet, the launch command, and the manifest's entry_point. .github/workflows/mcpb.yml Builds and smoke-tests on a PR that touches the bundle's inputs; on a published release, attaches the bundle to it. scripts/qa_launch_mcpb.py QA aid for TC-I68: runs the bundle's mcp_config the way a host does. tests/test_mcpb_manifest.py Version stamping, identity, user_config wiring, the allowlist, and staging from HEAD (against a throwaway repo).

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
uv server type, not python. The python type needs the dependencies vendored into the bundle, and the spec says compiled ones (pydantic, cryptography, Pillow) can't be bundled portably. The uv type ships pyproject.toml and uv.lock, and the host installs them.

mcp_config is explicit. The spec's prose calls it optional for uv, but the v0.4 validator that mcpb pack runs requires it (mcpb#263). It runs uv run --directory ${__dirname} --frozen --no-dev python -m mcp_gee_sweet. --frozen installs exactly what uv.lock pins, with no re-resolve on the user's machine; --no-dev leaves out the dev group (mkdocs, pytest, ruff). -m rather than a script path: running src/mcp_gee_sweet/__main__.py as a script puts the package directory first on sys.path, where server.py, cache.py and auth.py would shadow any top-level module of those names.

Version stamped at build time. pyproject.toml's version is dynamic (uv-dynamic-versioning, from the git tag), and a bundle has no .git, so the installed package reported the 0.0.0 fallback (checked). The staged manifest gets version, and an mcp_config.env UV_DYNAMIC_VERSIONING_BYPASS that the plugin uses instead of a tag, from --version (the release workflow passes the tag) or else server.json. The committed manifest.json carries neither, so no release step bumps it and nothing can drift (PR #1255 QA round 1; an earlier version kept both by hand and checked them against the tag). --smoke checks that the installed package reports the stamped version.

Staged from committed files on an allowlist, never the repo root. A working checkout holds credentials.json, token.json, service_account.json and src/mcp_gee_sweet/.env. mcpb pack excludes .env* by default but not the JSON files, and a deny-list in .mcpbignore would miss the next new one. So build_mcpb.py writes six root files, everything under src/mcp_gee_sweet/, and the icon into a temporary directory, reading each one from HEAD (git ls-tree, git show), and packs that. An untracked file, or an uncommitted edit to a tracked one, can't reach the bundle; the build warns about uncommitted changes it left out. mcpb pack . from the repo root isn't a supported build.

OAuth only. The bundle sets AUTH_METHOD=oauth. Asking for an OAuth client file states the user's intent, and the default waterfall would fall through to Application Default Credentials on a machine with gcloud set up, instead of offering consent. Service-account and ADC setups keep the manual config in docs/client-setup.md.

Token location. TOKEN_PATH is fixed at ${HOME}/.mcp-gee-sweet-token.json rather than asked for: - A file picker doesn't promise to accept a path that doesn't exist yet, and the token doesn't exist before the first consent. - The reference implementation (getMcpConfigForManifest) substitutes a user_config default into mcp_config without expanding the variables inside it, so a ${HOME}/... default would reach the server verbatim. ${HOME} written directly in mcp_config is expanded. - write_token_json doesn't create a parent directory, so the path has to be one that exists. ${HOME} does. - It's outside the extension directory, which an update replaces.

Optional settings need a default. An unset user_config value with no default is left as the literal ${user_config.KEY} text (replaceVariables keeps a variable it can't resolve). ENABLED_TOOLS therefore defaults to "", which the server reads as "every tool". CACHE_TTL isn't offered: MCPB has no integer type, int() of a decimal at import would stop the server, and set_cache_ttl changes it at runtime anyway.

Platforms. darwin and linux, what's tested. win32 waits for a Windows test. No compatibility.claude_desktop floor: the first Claude Desktop version with uv-type support isn't published (mcpb#291 says env passing was fixed in Claude Desktop, without a version).

docs.title: Not covered by automation
docs.text: Completing OAuth consent needs a person at a browser, and a Claude Desktop install needs macOS with Claude Desktop. Both are TC-I68 in docs/qa/tests/infra.md.

docs.title: Module implementation history
docs.text:
Per-PR history behind the rules in the root CLAUDE.md: review rounds, reversed approaches, live-QA findings, and the incident behind each rule. It was moved here verbatim from CLAUDE.md in #849 so that file could hold only the lasting rules and invariants, which cost every session ~24k tokens at its old size.

Each section below is the full original text of one CLAUDE.md entry, under the name CLAUDE.md uses for it. Entries short enough to have no history stayed in CLAUDE.md unchanged and aren't repeated here. Read the section for a module before changing that module's behavior: the invariants in CLAUDE.md are the summary, and the reasoning and edge cases are here.

Issue and PR numbers are as they were at the move (2026-09-29). Later history belongs in the module's own design or decision doc, not appended here.

docs.title: tools/drive/files.py
docs.text: tools/drive/files.py — file/folder operations (create_spreadsheet, import_csv_to_sheet, list_spreadsheets, list_files, search_files, create_folder, create_shortcut, copy_file, move_file, rename_file, star_file, unstar_file, delete_file, restore_file, empty_trash, list_shared_with_me, list_recent_files, get_storage_quota, etc.). star_file/unstar_file (#139) set starred via files().update — get_file_metadata, list_files, search_files, and search_spreadsheets all surface the starred field back (#388), and star_file/unstar_file mark the file's parent folder(s) dirty in drive_folder_cache the same way rename_file does, so a subsequent list_files reflects the new state without a manual refresh_cache (see TC-D202/203/260 in docs/qa/tests/drive_files.md). Both list_files and get_file_metadata now surface Drive's md5Checksum field as md5_checksum (#274) — None for Google Workspace files (Docs/Sheets/Slides have no fixed byte content, so the Drive API omits the field for them), a real hash for binary files. Exists so callers can detect real content drift instead of inferring it from modifiedTime, which sync/upload paths don't always keep faithful to actual content (see transfer.py's sync_folder use_checksum param below, the primary consumer of this).

docs.title: tools/drive/transfer.py
docs.text: tools/drive/transfer.py — upload/download/sync/export/revisions; _upload_local_file (the core behind the upload_local_file tool) is a module-level helper so docs/images.py's insert_local_images can call it directly, imported cross-package the same way docs/content.py imports _SA_QUOTA_ERROR from tools/drive/__init__.py. upload_local_file's convert param (#188) requests Drive's native import conversion — CSV/XLSX→Sheets, DOCX/MD/HTML→Docs, PPTX→Slides — by uploading with the source format's mimeType while setting the destination's mimeType metadata to the target Google Workspace type (_CONVERT_MIME maps extension → (source mime, target mime)). This is a different mechanism from docs/content.py's create_doc_from_file, which parses the file locally and rebuilds it via Docs API requests instead of Drive's importer — don't conflate the two when adding new conversion paths. sync_folder's convert_markdown param (#211) applies the same native-conversion mechanism to local .md files during sync uploads. Because the converted Doc keeps its .md name in Drive, _sync_level's drive_map-building loop matches it back to the local .md file directly (bypassing the export_format-suffix scheme normal Workspace files need) so resyncs settle into "in sync" instead of re-uploading a duplicate every run — this also reopens matching for a drive-only converted Doc with no local counterpart and no export_format (previously unreachable, since such files were always excluded from drive_map) — the plan-building loop classifies that case as a conflict (a convert_markdown Doc has no reverse conversion) before it ever reaches the download branch, so the download branch's own _EXPORT_MIME[None] guard is defensive-only dead code in the current implementation, not a reachable path (confirmed live: TC-D221). There is no reverse conversion (Doc → markdown). A converted Doc is recognized on every later sync via a Drive properties marker (_CONVERT_MARKDOWN_SOURCE_PROP) stamped at creation time by both _sync_level's own upload path and _upload_local_file's convert=True path (#414 rounds 2-3) — recognition is deliberately independent of whether the current call passes convert_markdown/convert, since the Doc's own persisted property is what matters, not this call's flag. Both paths stamp through the shared _convert_properties helper, which keeps every value within Drive's 124-byte per-property cap: _CONVERT_MARKDOWN_SOURCE_PROP holds the raw name only when it fits, and the generic _CONVERT_SOURCE_PROP marker (#769) falls back to a sha256: digest. _sync_level used to stamp the raw name directly, so a .md name over 95 bytes failed create() with 403 propertyLengthLimitExceeded after Drive had already made the Doc, leaving an orphan on every run (#805). Recognition goes through _converted_md_source_name, which accepts either key. The legacy markdown key is still honored, so Docs converted before #805 keep matching. The generic marker counts only for a .md source, and a digest is resolved against the Doc's own display name, which keeps its .md suffix. Because of that, a digest-marked Doc (a name over 103 UTF-8 bytes, .md included) stops matching if it's renamed in Drive; see docs/known-limitations.md. Three further edge cases from that round-3 review shipped as issue #422: the drive_map-building loop now detects (rather than silently resolving) a name collision between a plain file and a converted Doc, reporting it under failed instead of letting whichever is listed last win the slot and make the other invisible to the sync; _upload_local_file now stamps modifiedTime from the local file's mtime on a converted Doc (via create() then a metadata-only update(), mirroring _sync_level's own create() branch, since Drive's native import-conversion overwrites the create()-time value once conversion finishes) so a subsequent sync_folder lands in skipped rather than conflicts; and the drive-only branch now checks direction before _is_converted_md, so direction='upload' reports a plain skip like any other drive-only file instead of always reporting conflict. PR #433's own review round found the collision guard needed to go further: it originally only fired when the two colliding entries' _is_converted_md differed (a plain file vs. a converted Doc, #422's own reported shape), silently overwriting a same-type collision (two plain files, or two converted Docs, sharing a name) the exact same way; it now fires on any duplicate name regardless of type. The collision case is also now routed through the normal plan/action machinery (a new "collision" action, mapped to conflict during dry_run and to a real failed entry — kind: "collision_fail" — once execution is actually attempted) rather than writing to failed directly from the drive_map-building loop: that direct write both leaked into failed during dry_run (breaking the "dry_run never reports failures, only previews" invariant the pre-existing folder-collision failure path already upholds) and silently dropped a local file sharing the colliding name from every result list, since the plan loop's bare continue skipped it with zero acknowledgment. Separately, _upload_local_file's create()+update() pair now shares one broad except Exception returning {"error": ...} (matching _sync_level._run_one's own create+update pattern) instead of only catching quota HttpErrors and letting everything else — including a failure in the new metadata-only restamp update(), after create() already succeeded — propagate uncaught to upload_local_file, which has no try/except of its own. Issue #420 found that same broad except still lost information on the restamp-failure path specifically: a bare {"error": ...} (or, for _sync_level._run_one's own mirrored pair, a bare upload_fail) gave no way to find the Doc that create() had already genuinely made in Drive before the restamp failed — an untracked orphan. Fixed in both places by giving the restamp update() its own dedicated try/except that reports the created file's own ID alongside the error — _upload_local_file as {"error": ..., "fileId": ...}, _run_one as {"kind": "upload_fail", "name": ..., "error": ..., "fileId": ...} — while a create() failure still reports no fileId, correctly, since nothing was created. The two functions structure this differently: _run_one's restamp try/except sits nested inside its one broad outer try (which also covers create() and the if name in drive_map update branch above it), while _upload_local_file's is a separate, sequential try/except reached only after the create() try/except has already returned successfully — not nested inside it (PR #645 QA round 1 caught this file's prose originally describing both as nested). PR #650 factored the two restamp-failure branches' shared shape — the created Drive file {id!r} but failed to restamp its modifiedTime message plus storageQuotaExceeded→_SA_QUOTA_ERROR rendering — into a module-level _restamp_failure_result(file_id, exc) returning {"error": ..., "fileId": ...}; _run_one spreads that and layers its own kind/name keys on top. Before this only the create() except recognized a quota error — the restamp except caught bare Exception and would have leaked a raw str(e) for a quota failure there, unlike every other quota-error site in the file. sync_folder's and upload_local_folder's own failed-list aggregation steps (which previously narrowed each per-item result down to just {name, error}) were updated to carry fileId through when present, or the fix would have been invisible by the time a caller saw the result — and, since a fileId-carrying failure means create() genuinely changed the folder's contents, all three call sites (_sync_level, the upload_local_file tool, upload_local_folder) also had to treat that case as cache-dirtying, the same as a real success: none of them originally did (same QA round), since a fileId-carrying result still fell into each site's own success-only cache-invalidation gate's "false" branch. sync_folder's use_checksum param (#274) adds a content check ahead of _sync_level's mtime comparison for names present on both sides: when the local file's md5 (_local_md5, streamed in 1 MiB chunks) matches Drive's own md5Checksum (now fetched by _list_drive_children), the pair is treated as in sync regardless of modifiedTime drift — this is what actually fixes upload_local_file not stamping modifiedTime (unlike _sync_level's own upload path) causing a spurious re-download of identical content on the next sync, not just a same-mtime coincidence. Only applies where Drive returns a real md5Checksum — Workspace files and convert_markdown Docs have none and always fall back to mtime-only comparison, flag or no flag. A checksum mismatch doesn't force any decision by itself; it just falls through to the same mtime-based upload/download/conflict logic used when use_checksum=False, since content differing doesn't by itself say which side is newer. PR #472's own review round found four issues in this first version: the checksum comparison ran unconditionally, before the (cheap) mtime diff, including for pairs already within _SYNC_MTIME_TOLERANCE and even during dry_run=True — fixed by moving the mtime diff first and gating the hash read on use_checksum and not dry_run and abs(diff) > _SYNC_MTIME_TOLERANCE, so an already-in-sync pair or a dry_run preview never pays for a read it can't change the outcome of (#716 later dropped the abs(diff) part of that gate; see below); _local_md5 had no try/except unlike every other per-item operation in this module, so a file that became unreadable (deleted, permission-denied) between the directory scan and the hash read raised uncaught out of the whole sync_folder call instead of degrading to one failed entry — fixed via a new plan action (now "local_read_fail", which since PR #841 also covers the plan's own stat()) mirroring the existing "collision" pattern; and _upload_local_file's plain (non-convert) branch was identified as the actual root cause worth fixing directly — it never stamped modifiedTime the way the convert_mime branch three lines above already did (and #422 already established for that branch), so a file uploaded through it always read as "Drive newer" on the very next sync_folder regardless of content — now stamped unconditionally in the create() body for every upload (no follow-up update() needed for the plain case, since Drive only overwrites modifiedTime when import-conversion is involved). use_checksum remains valuable beyond that root-cause fix for causes of drift the mtime stamp doesn't cover (e.g. a local overwrite that happens to preserve mtime). One review finding was accepted as a known tradeoff rather than fixed: a checksum mismatch that resolves to 'upload' reads the local file twice (once to hash, once via MediaFileUpload for the actual transfer) — avoiding it would mean buffering the whole file in memory to share across both reads, a worse tradeoff for large files than one extra (likely page-cache-warm) disk read. Issue #659 covered the inverse of use_checksum's target failure mode — false sameness, where the two mtimes agree but the content has diverged (classic cause: a rename-in-place, since mv preserves mtime), which short-circuited to "in sync" before the hash block (then guarded on abs(diff) > _SYNC_MTIME_TOLERANCE) could run, so use_checksum=True couldn't reach it by construction (until #716, below). Fixed with a near-free discriminator in _sync_level's both-sides branch: size is now also fetched by _list_drive_children, and a within-tolerance mtime pair whose local st_size disagrees with Drive's reported size is not skipped — it is reported as a conflict for every direction, never an auto-transfer (PR #712 QA round 1): the mtimes agree so recency is unknown, and the diff-based branches already report conflict rather than overwrite a target they can tell is newer, so this branch — which knows less — must be at least as cautious. The byte-size check is one stat() and no read, so unlike the hash block it runs during dry_run too. Non-Workspace files only (size, like md5Checksum, is absent for Workspace/convert_markdown files). A same-size content edit that also preserves mtime still reads as "in sync" under the default use_checksum=False. Issue #716 closed that gap for an explicit use_checksum=True: it now hashes every both-sides pair with a Drive md5Checksum, within tolerance or not (a size mismatch is still settled from the stat() alone, first). A within-tolerance hash mismatch is a conflict for every direction, the same as the size mismatch; both come from _diverged_same_mtime_step. The hashes run after the plan loop, concurrently, capped at _SYNC_HASH_CONCURRENCY, each filling in a placeholder step that holds the mtime-only fallback from _mtime_step. dry_run still never hashes, and an affected step's reason ends in (checksum not verified in dry_run), since the real run can decide differently. upload_local_folder (#411) used to have its own independent inline upload loop with no convert param, unreachable from _upload_local_file's conversion mechanism — bulk-importing a folder of CSV/DOCX/PPTX into native Workspace formats required falling back to per-file upload_local_file calls. Fixed by routing each candidate through _upload_local_file itself, gaining the same convert param and its semantics (an unsupported extension lands in failed rather than uploading as-is, matching upload_local_file's own error-not-silent-fallback behavior). The existing bulk skip_if_exists pre-check (one list() call for the whole folder, not one per file — TC-D100) is preserved rather than replaced by _upload_local_file's own per-call check: the folder loop now fetches each existing file's mimeType alongside its name in that same single call, decides skip-worthiness itself (name-only match when convert=False; name and target-mimeType match when convert=True, mirroring _upload_local_file's own convert-aware duplicate check), and then calls _upload_local_file with skip_if_exists=False for whatever survives — so existence is never checked twice. sync_folder(dry_run=True)'s response used to duplicate every skip/conflict name into both a flat list (skipped/conflicts) and a full {name, action, reason} entry in actions, deterministically tripping the response-size cap on a moderately-sized, mostly-in-sync folder even though actions alone (name + action-type + reason for every item, including upload/download entries the flat lists never populated during dry_run in the first place) was already a complete, non-redundant picture (issue #512). Fixed by leaving uploaded/downloaded/skipped/conflicts/failed empty during dry_run rather than trimming or toggling actions itself. Separately, sync_folder previously had no response-size-cap bypass at all (local_path_available=False) unlike every other capped tool except export_file/list_file_activity (both deliberately, per the decision doc below) — its own local_path param already means the sync destination, so it can't double as a dump target the way get_sheet_data's local_path does. Fixed by adding a separate result_local_path param following the same unconditional-if-passed write_capped_result_to_disk pattern as every other capped tool with a bypass; enforce_response_size_cap gained a local_path_param override so its error message names the right parameter instead of hardcoding local_path. PR #518's own QA review round live-caught a gap in that first version: result_local_path had no guard against pointing at or inside local_path — since local_path is scanned as sync input on every call (unlike every other capped tool's local_path/result_local_path, which are pure output destinations), a manifest written there showed up as a new local-only file on the very next sync and would have been uploaded to Drive on a real run. Fixed by rejecting the call up front (ValueError, before any Drive API call) when Path(result_local_path).resolve() equals or is a descendant of the resolved local_path. upload_file's convert_to_doc param implements the identical native-import-conversion trick as _upload_local_file's convert/_CONVERT_MIME above, independently — raw text/markdown/html content instead of a local file, always targeting a Doc since there's no file extension to dispatch Sheets/Slides on — with no cross-reference between the two (issue #412). Fixed by sharing _GOOGLE_DOC_MIME as the single source of truth for the target mimeType literal both mechanisms write, plus explicit docstring cross-references at both call sites; the two code paths themselves stayed separate rather than being merged, since their actual upload semantics (raw content vs. local file, single target vs. extension-dispatched) differ enough that unifying them would cost more complexity than it'd save. Issue #424 (folded #421's two extra findings in) was pure hardening on this same convert_markdown matching logic, no behavior change: the synthetic "_is_converted_md" key spread into every drive_map entry (previously read directly at 5 separate call sites — the pattern PR #433's own review round flagged as having already caused one missed site) was replaced with _is_converted_md_entry(f), a helper that recomputes the classification on demand from the resource's own mimeType/properties rather than caching it — drive_map is now a plain passthrough of Drive's file resource shape again, and every call site (the build loop, both plan conflict branches, the upload-execution reimport check, the download-execution guard) shares one place to agree with when this classification's rules change. The three independently-hand-written "no reverse conversion" messages (drive-only plan conflict, drive-newer plan conflict, download-execution guard) now interpolate a shared _NO_REVERSE_CONVERSION_CLAUSE constant instead. The dead assert convert_source is not None fell out naturally once the build loop's local_name derivation was rewritten against the new helper. The upload-execution branch's _CONVERT_MIME[".md"] unpack moved inside the convert_this check so it's only looked up for an actual .md conversion, not unconditionally for every upload. The doubled create()+update() latency on every new converted-.md upload (both here and in _upload_local_file's convert=True path) was reviewed and left as an accepted tradeoff, not fixed — Drive's import-conversion finishes asynchronously after create() already returns, so there's no single call that can request both the upload and the post-conversion modifiedTime restamp together, and polling for conversion completion before restamping would trade one predictable extra call for an unpredictable number of slower ones. Issue #814 took converted .md Docs off the modifiedTime comparison entirely: Drive updates a Doc's modifiedTime from the Docs backend asynchronously, minutes behind, which both overwrote the restamp (an unedited Doc sat in conflicts) and hid real Drive edits for minutes. Every converted-.md upload now stamps _CONVERTED_MD_SOURCE_MTIME_PROP (the local mtime), a re-upload also stamps _CONVERTED_MD_BASELINE_REV_PROP (the Doc's latest revision, read just before the update()) and clears _CONVERTED_MD_IMPORT_REV_PROP, and the first sync afterward records the import's revision ID there. _sync_level then judges the local side against the stamped mtime and the Drive side from revisions.list (_converted_md_drive_state/_converted_md_step, fetched concurrently after the plan loop and capped at _SYNC_REVISION_CONCURRENCY, during dry_run too). A Drive edit is always a conflict, including when the local file changed too (previously an upload over the Drive edit). A revision-read failure is a "drive_read_fail" plan action. A Doc without the stamp (converted before #814) keeps the modifiedTime path until its next re-upload. The restamp stays, now cosmetic for these Docs, and the import-revision write re-sends the stamped modifiedTime, since a property-only update bumps it to "now" (seen live). PR #854 QA round 1 tightened it: the source-mtime stamp keeps microsecond precision and is compared exactly (_CONVERTED_MD_STAMP_TOLERANCE), since the 5s Drive clock-skew tolerance hid a local save made within 5s of the upload. The import-revision write always re-sends a modifiedTime, since a property write bumps it to "now": the stamped source mtime for an unedited Doc, and Drive's own listed value for a Drive-edited one (re-sending the source mtime there erased the edit's timestamp). It also marks the folder cache dirty. An empty revision history is a drive_read_fail, not an edit. A local change under direction='download' is a conflict even while the import is pending. The upload path's fresh revision read now aborts the upload as a conflict if the latest revision moved since planning. Every upload also stamps _CONVERTED_MD_UPLOADED_AT_PROP, so a pruned baseline falls back to finding the import by timestamp, and a candidate import more than _CONVERTED_MD_IMPORT_WINDOW after the upload is read as the import merged into a later edit (changed). Legacy Docs already stuck in the drift conflict are unstuck by touching the local file (docs/known-limitations.md). Design: docs/decisions/decision-converted-doc-change-detection.md; other conversion types are #818.

docs.title: tools/docs/content.py
docs.text: docs/content.py — helpers (_md_to_html, _to_doc_requests, _html_to_doc_requests) and tools (create_doc, get_doc_content, write_doc_content, create_doc_from_file, update_doc_from_file, get_doc_structure, find_in_doc). insert_doc_text/delete_doc_range/insert_page_break/insert_softbreak_paragraph moved to docs/editing.py, and insert_inline_image/insert_local_images moved into docs/images.py (#372, following #371's extraction of named_ranges.py) — _collect_doc_paragraphs moved alongside them into docs/indices.py, next to its own sibling low-level helper utf16_len, and the dead _html_to_text helper (no callers anywhere in the codebase, confirmed via a repo-wide grep before deleting it) was dropped rather than moved. update_doc_from_file (#341) combines create_doc_from_file's server-side file reading (extension inference to markdown/html, or an explicit content_format override) with write_doc_content's in-place clear+replace — the clear-then-insert mechanism (including the same-batch insertText style-inheritance quirk described below) was extracted out of write_doc_content into a shared _replace_doc_content helper so both tools have exactly one implementation of it, the same way _apply_doc_content is already shared by create_doc/create_doc_from_file/write_doc_content. find_in_doc searches paragraph text (including table cells) and returns start_index/end_index offsets in UTF-16 code units usable directly with style_doc_range — _collect_doc_paragraphs is a generator (so a caller can stop early once max_results is hit) that walks the Docs API body, trusting each ParagraphElement's own startIndex when present and otherwise carrying the running offset forward rather than dropping that element, since the API doesn't always populate it (seen on a document's first element). get_doc_structure now also surfaces each paragraph's headingId (paragraphStyle.headingId) — confirmed live present on the default single-tab documents.get() response for both TITLE/SUBTITLE and HEADING_1..6 paragraphs, no includeTabsContent needed. create_doc/create_doc_from_file/write_doc_content now run an automatic second pass (_resolve_heading_anchors, gated by the cheap _has_pending_anchor_links check so content with no #-links skips the extra API round trip entirely) after any conversion that left a GitHub/GitLab-style #slug heading-anchor link behind (issue #409): it resolves the anchor against the doc's own real headings via anchors.resolve_heading_anchor and rewrites it to a working .../edit?tab=t.0#heading=<headingId> jump link (an ordinary URL is sufficient — no Link.headingId API field needed, confirmed live), or strips the link (keeping the text plain) when no heading matches with reasonable confidence — a link silently pointing at the wrong section is worse than a plain, unlinked mention. This was a deliberate product decision to resolve anchors automatically rather than only exposing headingId and leaving matching to the calling agent — see docs/design/heading-anchor-resolution.md for the full rationale. PR #453's own QA round (/code-review high + live testing against a fixture with no table and no anchor on the doc's first element) caught two correctness bugs the first version's hand-rolled body walk had: it only inspected top-level paragraph elements (a heading or anchor link living inside a table cell was invisible to both _has_pending_anchor_links and _resolve_heading_anchors), and it required a run's own pe.get("startIndex")/endIndex to both be non-None (silently dropping an anchor that is, or is part of, the document's first body element — the Docs API omits startIndex there, the same quirk _collect_doc_paragraphs already handles). Fixed by _walk_headings_and_anchor_runs, a dedicated recursive walker mirroring _collect_doc_paragraphs's own two correctness properties (table-cell recursion; carrying the running offset forward via character-by-character advance rather than trusting a run's own possibly-inconsistent endIndex) rather than reusing _collect_doc_paragraphs itself, since that generator's yielded shape (text + char-indices only) doesn't carry per-run link URLs or heading-paragraph style info and is used elsewhere (find_in_doc) in a way not worth risking a signature change for. _has_pending_anchor_links gained a second parameter (tables: list[Table], walked via _table_has_pending_anchor_link, recursing into nested tables) since fill_tables() builds and executes table-cell requests separately from content_requests, invisible to the original single-argument guard. create_doc/create_doc_from_file/write_doc_content now support inline images in markdown (![alt](src)) and HTML (<img>) conversion (issue #333) via a shared _apply_doc_content helper: src may be a local filesystem path (uploaded to Drive), a drive:<file_id> reference to an already-uploaded file, or a public http(s):// URL (used directly) — resolved by _resolve_image_source, sharing local-path/drive: sources anyone:reader the same way insert_local_images already does, then (per explicit product decision, and now also insert_local_images's own default — a behavior change from its original #332 shipped version) revoking that temporary share once the image is embedded, unless revoke_sharing=False. The Docs API rejects an entire batchUpdate atomically if any one insertInlineImage request in it can't be fetched (confirmed live via TC-DOC102's own deliberately-unreachable-URL case) — _apply_doc_content retries with the failing request stripped (its index is parsed directly out of Google's own error message) rather than losing every other request in the same call; see docs/design/image-conversion.md for the full design, including why Image is a zero-width AST node (not a marker) and the deliberate table-cell-image gap.

docs.title: tools/docs/editing.py
docs.text: docs/editing.py — tools (insert_doc_text, delete_doc_range, insert_page_break, insert_softbreak_paragraph), extracted out of content.py (#372) as content.py's text-range editing primitives, distinct from that file's remaining whole-document create/read/write concern. insert_softbreak_paragraph joins multiple lines with a literal "\v" (vertical tab) character in a single insertText call — confirmed live that the Docs API stores this as one paragraph element rather than splitting it, matching the Docs UI's own Shift+Enter soft-break convention — and sets namedStyleType explicitly over the inserted span rather than leaving it to whatever the insertion point would otherwise inherit.

docs.title: tools/docs/images.py
docs.text: docs/images.py — tools (insert_inline_image, insert_local_images) plus inline-image size validation/downscaling/error-clarification shared by every insertInlineImage call site (issue #400). The two tools moved here from content.py (#372) rather than into a differently-named module — issue #372 predates #400's creation of this file, and by the time it was picked up, images.py already existed here for the size-validation helpers, so merging avoided colliding with a newly-invented module name (an earlier version of this rationale claimed the two tools were already this module's "primary callers"; that doesn't hold up — content.py's own _resolve_image_source, which stays there, depends on the same shared helpers just as heavily). insert_local_images uploads local image files and swaps each into the doc at a plain-text marker in one call; confirmed live that insertInlineImage with a drive_file_id fails with "There was a problem retrieving the image" unless the file is first shared anyone/reader — the Docs backend fetches the image as an anonymous HTTP request, so being accessible to the authenticated user alone is not enough (this also applies to insert_inline_image's own drive_file_id path). Google Docs rejects any inline image over ~25 megapixels or ~50MB with a bare HttpError 400 "...The provided image is too large." naming neither the actual limit nor the image's own size (confirmed against Google's documented ceiling: https://developers.google.com/workspace/docs/api/how-tos/images, 25 megapixels / 50MB / PNG-JPEG-GIF only). check_dimensions/check_image_file pre-validate and return a clear {"error": ...} naming the limit and the image's actual size before any upload/share/embed call happens; downscale_image_bytes (Pillow — see docs/decisions/decision-pillow-image-dependency.md for why it was added as a dependency) resizes in place, preserving format, and declines (None) rather than corrupting an animated GIF (Image.resize only touches the current frame). check_image_file (then check_image_bytes, a bytes-in predecessor replaced in #560) originally only enforced the megapixel limit, not the byte-size one the module's own docstring already cited — a low-compressibility image (e.g. noise data) could be well under 25 megapixels but still over 50MB, passing pre-validation silently and only failing at the real batchUpdate call (issue #562, confirmed live via a real ~75MB-but-24-megapixel PNG). Fixed by adding check_file_size/too_large_bytes_message (the byte-size counterpart to check_dimensions/too_large_message) into it, and extending downscale_image_bytes with a bounded iterative shrink loop for the case where the megapixel-based scale factor alone is a no-op (the image is already within that limit) but the encoded result is still over the byte limit — unlike pixel count, encoded byte size isn't predictable from a single scale factor since it depends on compression, not just dimensions. The two Drive-metadata-only size checks (insert_inline_image's drive_file_id path here, _resolve_image_source's drive: path in content.py) were consolidated into one shared check_drive_image_metadata helper reading both imageMediaMetadata and Drive's own size field, replacing what had been the same check_dimensions-only pattern duplicated across both files. PR #580's own QA round 1 caught that rewrite_too_large_error — the fallback for uri-sourced images, which skip pre-validation entirely — still only named the 25-megapixel limit, even though a byte-size-caused rejection could now reach it too; since Google's raw error text doesn't say which limit was actually hit and this call site never fetched the bytes to check, the message was made limit-agnostic (names both ceilings) rather than guessing which one applies. insert_inline_image's drive_file_id path, insert_local_images' local_path entries, and _resolve_image_source's drive:/local-path branches (content.py) all gained an opt-in auto_downscale param (default False, fail-fast with the clear error) wired to this module — a drive_file_id/drive: source that gets downscaled creates a new " (resized)"-suffixed copy alongside the original via downscale_drive_file (the original file is never mutated), while a local-path source just uploads the resized bytes directly via upload_and_share_image instead of the original file, since there's no pre-existing Drive artifact to avoid colliding with. Issue #560 deduplicated those call sites: downscale_drive_file takes the source's own Drive metadata and owns the resized copy's parent-folder fallback, and prepare_local_image owns the local-path check→downscale→upload sequence, so insert_inline_image, insert_local_images, and _resolve_image_source each only record the outcome. check_image_file reads just stat() and the image header, never the full file or its pixels, so an under-limit local image is read from disk once, by the upload itself. For PNG/JPEG/GIF it constructs Pillow's format plugin directly instead of going through Image.open, whose decompression-bomb guard would otherwise make a header claiming more than ~179 megapixels unreadable and silently skip pre-validation (PR #801 QA round 1); the file itself is opened outside the best-effort guard, so an unreadable file still reports a read error rather than passing as "not an image." downscale_image_bytes runs via asyncio.to_thread, since a full decode + resize + re-encode is CPU-heavy. Deliberately out of scope: a bare http(s):// image source (either insert_inline_image's own uri param or a markdown/HTML ![alt](http://...)/<img src="http://...">) — pre-validating or auto-downscaling it would mean fetching arbitrary external content just to check it, and re-hosting a resized copy somewhere Google can fetch it from is a bigger behavior change than this fix warrants. That source kind instead gets rewrite_too_large_error's fallback: Google's own "too large" HttpError message is caught and rewritten with the same limit/size explanation once the embed actually fails, rather than staying opaque.

docs.title: tools/docs/anchors.py
docs.text: docs/anchors.py — resolve_heading_anchor, the pure slug-matching logic behind the anchor-resolution pass above. Tries GitHub's non-collapsing hyphen convention (hand-rolled — no known Python package reproduces it) and GitLab's collapsing convention (delegated to python-markdown's own toc extension slugify, already a project dependency, confirmed live to collapse hyphens the same way) against the document's full heading list, with GitHub/GitLab-style numeric -1/-2 duplicate-heading disambiguation applied before matching; falls back to normalized word-token comparison for a slug that doesn't exactly match either scheme. Deliberately does not try to detect which generator produced a given anchor up front — see the design doc for why. Has an inline TODO(#409 follow-up) flagging the cascading try-each-scheme approach as a first pass, not the most precise/efficient possible mechanism. The same QA round (PR #453) found the fuzzy fallback could silently resolve to the wrong heading: it unconditionally stripped a trailing -<digits> from the anchor before comparing, even when those digits were genuine heading wording rather than a dedup suffix, and its match loop returned the first heading with matching normalized tokens with no regard for which duplicate a stripped suffix actually pointed at — directly contradicting the feature's own "a wrong link is worse than no link" design goal. Fixed via _fuzzy_match/_match_tokens_at_occurrence: the anchor's literal tokens (with any trailing digits intact) are tried first at occurrence 0 — safe, since GitHub/GitLab give a duplicate heading's first occurrence the bare/unsuffixed slug, so a suffix-free anchor naming a duplicated heading still resolves correctly without ever needing to strip anything — and only if that fails, and the anchor ends in -<digits>, is the suffix stripped and its number used as the required occurrence index among headings sharing the same normalized tokens; a requested occurrence that doesn't exist (e.g. a claimed 3rd duplicate when only one heading matches) returns None rather than guessing the nearest candidate.

docs.title: tools/docs/style.py
docs.text:
docs/style.py — helpers (_NAMED_STYLE_TYPES, _read_body_styles, _read_named_styles, _build_named_style_requests, _text_style_and_fields) and tools (style_doc_range, style_doc_table_cells, create_paragraph_bullets, delete_paragraph_bullets, get_doc_theme, get_doc_named_styles, apply_theme). create_paragraph_bullets/delete_paragraph_bullets (#334) wrap the Docs API's createParagraphBullets/deleteParagraphBullets requests, previously only used internally by emitter.py's markdown-to-Doc conversion, as caller-facing tools for fixing list membership/nesting on paragraphs already in a doc — get_doc_structure had no way to even detect a flattened nested list (the AST emitter's own conversion bug from the same issue), and there was no way to fix one afterward short of delete-and-retype as plain text. createParagraphBullets has no nestingLevel field of its own — same constraint the emitter already works around (see that file's own long comment) — the API infers a paragraph's depth purely from its own leading tab characters at call time, consuming them once applied; create_paragraph_bullets reproduces that mechanism per range (insertText-ing nesting_level tab characters before the range, then extending the range's endIndex to cover them) rather than exposing a fake nestingLevel parameter that doesn't correspond to any real request field. get_doc_structure (content.py) now also surfaces each paragraph's bullet field ({listId, nestingLevel} or null), normalizing a top-level item's absent nestingLevel to 0 so every list paragraph reports a level — this is what makes the flattened-list defect (#334's original report) detectable at all, and is the read half create_paragraph_bullets/delete_paragraph_bullets fix on the write side. PR #524's QA round found create_paragraph_bullets's first version didn't work at all on its own flagship use case (nesting paragraphs already in an existing list, #334's original repro): live-verified two compounding causes — createParagraphBullets is a no-op on a paragraph that's already part of a list (doesn't change its level, doesn't consume the signaling tab, which is left behind as literal text), and even after a deleteParagraphBullets+recreate, the API infers a paragraph's depth only relative to whatever else is included in that same call — a paragraph adjacent to an untouched, already-listed neighbor gets silently pulled back to that neighbor's level regardless of its own tabs (the same class of bug PR #432 fixed in emitter.py, confirmed live to also apply here). Fixed by always deleteParagraphBullets-ing a target paragraph first (harmless even if it wasn't previously listed), and — for a paragraph that's already part of a list — expanding the affected span to include its full contiguous run of same-listId neighbors (preserving each neighbor's own current nestingLevel unchanged) before issuing one createParagraphBullets call per contiguous same-preset run, mirroring emitter.py's own established grouping pattern. Confirmed live against the real API for both the multi-paragraph-range case (TC-DOC156) and an isolated single-paragraph target whose only same-list neighbor sits outside the requested range. A second QA round on the same PR caught a follow-on regression from that fix, also live-verified (Playwright): merging context/neighbor paragraphs into the run and applying one bulletPreset to the whole call meant an already-numbered list, repaired without the caller re-passing bullet_preset="NUMBERED_DECIMAL_ALPHA_ROMAN" explicitly, silently converted its untouched siblings to plain bullets — the tool's own hardcoded default (BULLET_DISC_CIRCLE_SQUARE) always won. Fixed by reading the document's own lists map (document["lists"][listId]["listProperties"]["nestingLevels"][level]) to detect an already-listed paragraph's real style before choosing a run's preset — glyphType present means numbered, glyphSymbol present means bulleted, confirmed live for both — and preferring that inferred style over the hardcoded default whenever the caller didn't pass bullet_preset explicitly on any paragraph in the run; an explicit caller-supplied preset still always wins. Since context paragraphs no longer carry a fixed preset up front (it's resolved once per formed run, after grouping), a preset mismatch only forces a run split when it's between two paragraphs the caller explicitly gave conflicting presets to and they're immediately adjacent with no non-explicit paragraph bridging them; a conflict bridged by a shared context paragraph (both explicit ends expand into the same run via a same-listId neighbor between them) is instead reported as an {"error": ...} rather than silently picking one side. Issue #713 (a follow-up filed during PR #711's QA) found create_paragraph_bullets still had the exact nestingLevel 0 collapse emitter.py carried under #439: a formed run in which every paragraph sits at nesting_level >= 1 (no level-0 member — either only such ranges were passed, or the same-listId neighbor expansion pulled in only level-≥1 paragraphs) collapsed to nestingLevel 0 with the depth-0 disc glyph, indent bumped so it still looked nested. Fixed by porting emitter.py's #439 fix verbatim: such a run is wrapped with a throwaway 0-tab anchor paragraph (insertText "\n" at run_start → createParagraphBullets over the range extended by 1 → deleteContentRange the anchor), so the real items land at their true level; the insert (+1) and delete (−1) cancel, leaving positions outside the run untouched and the descending-run application order intact. _text_style_and_fields (shared by style_doc_range and editing.py's insert_softbreak_paragraph) used to clear a hyperlink by setting textStyle.link = {} — the Docs API rejects an empty Link object outright ("must include at least one type"), confirmed live, so link_url: null always failed instead of clearing (#408). Fixed by omitting the link key from textStyle entirely while still naming "link" in the field mask, the correct way to reset a nested message field to its default (no link) per Docs API fields-mask semantics — confirmed live this actually clears an existing link. Both call sites' own if text_style: requests.append(...) guard had to change to if fields: too: a link-clear-only call now legitimately produces an empty text_style dict with a non-empty fields list (["link"]), and the old guard would have silently skipped sending the request at all.
