Issue #448 factored the omit-key-but-mask-field trick itself out of _text_style_and_fields's inline link_url handling into a small, general _add_or_clear_field(text_style, fields, api_field, value) helper — content.py's heading-anchor-link resolve/strip code (_resolve_heading_anchors) had independently hand-rolled the identical two-line pattern for the same reason, with only a comment pointing back at style.py's prose to explain it; both now call the one shared helper, so a future nullable nested field (e.g. foreground_color: null) has a place to reuse this instead of a third hand-rolled copy, and the "why" lives in exactly one docstring instead of two comments that could drift out of sync.

Issue #1069 found create_paragraph_bullets added the requested nesting_level to a listed paragraph's current level instead of setting it: re-running a 0/1/2 call gave 0/2/4, and a call naming one paragraph also moved the neighbours the expansion pulled in. A live probe settled the cause. deleteParagraphBullets leaves no tab characters behind, but it keeps a level-N item's indent as indentStart = indentFirstLine = 36pt × N, and createParagraphBullets reads that indent as depth on top of the inserted tabs. Fixed by zeroing both indents over each run between its deleteParagraphBullets and its tab inserts; the new bullet sets its own indents afterward, so the reset is never visible. The #713 anchor wrap is unaffected: with the reset, the anchor and the items carry no leftover indent, so their tabs alone decide the run's minimum. A control run with the reset stripped reproduced the issue live (0/2/4, then compounding toward Docs' level cap of 8).

docs.title: tools/docs/doc_to_ast.py / docs/ast_to_markdown.py / docs/markdown_export.py
docs.text: docs/doc_to_ast.py / docs/ast_to_markdown.py / docs/markdown_export.py — the read-side counterpart to the Markdown write path above (issue #300): doc_to_ast.py walks a documents().get() response into the same AST (docs/ast.py) the write pipeline produces (headings, styled runs, nested/ordered/checked bullets via the same document["lists"][listId] glyph-info lookup style.py's create_paragraph_bullets already established, blockquotes inferred from the emitter's own indentStart+borderLeft signal, images via document["inlineObjects"], and tables including nesting via tableCellStyle.columnSpan/rowSpan); ast_to_markdown.py serializes that AST to Markdown, the inverse of html_parser.py's HTML→AST direction; markdown_export.py wires both into the get_doc_as_markdown tool, with an opt-in include_comments param that appends every non-resolved comment (author, quoted anchor, content, replies) via the same Drive comments resource comments.py uses. Deliberately built as a third AST pass rather than converting export_file(export_format='html')'s output through an HTML-to-Markdown library — Google's own Docs HTML export is heavily styled (redundant inline spans), which would need fragile cleanup heuristics to convert cleanly, whereas walking into this project's own AST reuses the exact mapping markdown-support.md already documents, just inverted. Both inline code and a fenced code block are written to the Docs API identically (a run, or every run in a paragraph, with font_family="Courier New" — no other marker), so ast_to_markdown.py treats a Paragraph as a fenced block only when every run in it is code-styled; a paragraph containing nothing but one inline code span (no other text) is genuinely indistinguishable from a one-line code block and renders as a fenced block either way — a documented format-level ambiguity, not a bug (see docs/known-limitations.md's get_doc_as_markdown entry). A nested table (a table inside a table cell) has no Markdown table syntax to express — the mirror image of markdown-support.md's identical write-side gap — so that cell renders a placeholder note instead of silently losing the inner table's content. Live round-trip verification (build a Doc via the existing write pipeline from a Markdown source covering every construct in scope, then read it back and diff) caught two bugs neither the hand-written unit tests nor a docs-API-shape assumption alone would have: a naive f"**{text}**" wrapper breaks CommonMark's emphasis-flanking rule when text has trailing whitespace ("**Bold **" doesn't close, renders as literal asterisks) — fixed by moving leading/trailing whitespace outside the style markers; and joining every block (including consecutive list items) with a blank line produced a needlessly "loose" list — fixed by joining consecutive BulletItem nodes with a single newline instead (CommonMark parses a loose list as the same list either way; this is a readability polish, not a correctness fix). See docs/design/doc-to-markdown.md for the full design writeup. PR #591 QA round 1 found two further narrow silent-content-loss gaps (#594), both in constructs the initial round-trip verification's fixture happened not to exercise: _is_code_block filters node.runs to Run items only before checking font_family, so an Image sitting in an otherwise all-Courier-New paragraph is invisible to the check — the paragraph still correctly renders as a fenced block, but the fenced-block render path then built its text from Run items only, dropping the Image with no trace. Fixed via _render_code_block, which walks node.runs in source order and renders each contiguous run of code text as its own fence with any interleaved Image rendered on its own line outside any fence (Markdown has no way to embed an image inside a fenced block), rather than silently losing whichever Image items were present. Separately, doc_to_ast.py's _cell_content_to_children used to continue past any table-cell paragraph with empty runs entirely — a deliberate blank-line spacer paragraph between two lines of real text (the identical runs=[] shape document_to_ast already produces for a body-level blank line, see test_paragraph_that_is_only_a_newline_becomes_empty_runs) silently merged its neighbors together with a single " " joiner instead of two, indistinguishable from a cell with no spacer at all. Fixed by no longer skipping an empty-runs paragraph in the seen_content/joiner bookkeeping: it contributes no text of its own but still counts as content once seen, so the next real paragraph still gets its own separate joiner on top of the blank paragraph's own — preserving the spacer as a second newline (rendered as a doubled <br> in _render_cell's pipe-table output) rather than collapsing it away. PR #599's own QA round 1 (live QA, not just code review) found that round-1 fix was still incomplete at cell edges: doc_to_ast.py already represented a leading or trailing spacer paragraph correctly, as a leading/trailing " " on the cell's joined text (confirmed via local AST inspection), but ast_to_markdown.py's _render_cell did text = "".join(parts).strip() before converting " " to "<br>" — .strip() silently ate exactly that edge newline, so only a spacer sandwiched between two real lines (the shape round 1's own new tests happened to cover) ever survived to the rendered Markdown. Fixed by reordering _render_cell to convert " " → "<br>" first and .strip() second: "<br>" isn't whitespace, so a spacer that's already been turned into a <br> marker survives the strip, while genuine incidental whitespace at the true edges still gets trimmed as before.

docs.title: tools/docs/html_parser.py
docs.text: docs/html_parser.py — HTML→AST. _AstParser.handle_data only buffers text while a block context is open (<p>/<li>/heading/table cell) — text with no wrapping block tag was silently dropped (#343). Fixed via a generic _tag_depth counter tracking open non-block tags: bare top-level text (depth 0, e.g. "hello world" with zero surrounding tags) now gets an implicit paragraph wrap, while text merely wrapped in an inline tag with no block ancestor (e.g. <span>no blocks</span>, depth 1) stays an intentional no-op, matching test_inline_only_html_skips_batchupdate. _finalize() (called once after parser.feed() in html_to_ast) flushes whatever block is still open at end-of-input, since the implicit paragraph never gets a real closing tag. _tag_depth excludes tags in _VOID_TAGS (br, img, hr, input, meta, link, area, base, embed, source, track, wbr, col) — Python's stdlib HTMLParser never synthesizes a close-tag call for a void element written without a self-closing slash (e.g. plain <img src="x">), so counting it would leave _tag_depth permanently stuck above 0 and silently re-drop all bare text for the rest of the document (caught in PR #385's own review round — the initial fix only excluded br by name). _emit_block_node (shared by the normal close-tag path, _interrupt_open_block, and _finalize) used to silently drop the entire node — not just the unsupported content — whenever a closed block's buffered runs came back completely empty (e.g. a <p> whose only child was an unhandled <img>), collapsing the paragraph boundary between its neighbors (#401). Fixed via a preserve_if_empty flag: the block's own first/only close now keeps an empty node (runs=[]) instead of dropping it, while a resumed frame's re-close (_block_resumed, set by _resume_interrupted_block) still uses the old skip-if-empty behavior, since an empty result there just means "no trailing text after the nested construct that interrupted this block," not "this tag was empty" — conflating the two reintroduced a spurious empty BulletItem for every <li>text<ul>...</ul></li> (no trailing text after the nested list), caught by the existing test_parent_text_survives_alongside_nested_list regression test. A bare top-level <hr> (python-markdown's rendering of both --- and ___ thematic breaks) never opens a block at all, so it's handled separately in handle_starttag: when no block is currently open, it appends an empty Paragraph node directly rather than falling through the inline-tag no-op path. emitter.py's ast_to_requests makes the matching runs-empty-vs-whitespace-only distinction, since its own if not text.strip(): continue guard would otherwise skip the now-empty node's contribution to full_text and lose the boundary anyway. Whitespace-only paragraphs (e.g. <p> </p> or a lone  ) were deliberately left dropped by that #401 fix as a separate, not-yet-fixed case — fixed under #402: markdown authors commonly write a standalone   line as a deliberate blank-line spacer (a literal blank line collapses between paragraphs), so a freshly-closed <p> (opened and closed with nothing in between, e.g. <p> </p>) now always keeps its whitespace-only-but-non-empty runs, unconditional on preserve_if_empty — there's real (if invisible) content here to lose, not just a boundary. This is deliberately scoped to tag == "p" specifically, not every tag _emit_block_node dispatches on: PR #441's own QA round live-caught a first version of the fix with no such scoping, which also preserved whitespace-only <li>/heading content — <li>Real</li><li> </li><li>More</li> rendered a real bullet glyph with only invisible content between two genuine list items, same for headings — since the blank-line-spacer convention this fix targets doesn't apply to list items or headings the same way. A resumed <p>'s own whitespace-only trailing flush also does NOT get the fresh-<p> treatment: an earlier version of this fix that didn't check self._block_resumed regressed test_nested_list_via_markdown_preserves_parent_text, since a resumed block's trailing whitespace (e.g. the indentation newline python-markdown emits between a nested list's </ul> and the outer <li>'s own </li>) is markup-formatting noise, not authored content. self._block_resumed (tracked since #401 but, per that fix's own history in docs/qa/tests/docs_content.md TC-DOC136, no longer gating anything there — preserve_if_empty/_block_had_unsupported_content replaced it for that purpose) is read again here for this new purpose. Both the non-<p> and resumed-<p> cases fall back to the same preserve_if_empty gate the runs=[] case already used. emitter.py was simplified to match: it no longer special-cases whitespace text at all, just emits whatever text a kept node carries — the empty-string (runs=[]) case still contributes only its trailing "\n". A resumed block's genuine trailing   (not markup-formatting noise) is a known, documented remaining gap — tracked as #444, not fixed here. handle_endtag's <ol>/<ul> close-tag handling used to pop self._list_ordered (the stack BulletItem.depth/.ordered are computed from) only when the closing tag's implied type matched the stack's own top entry — a mismatched pair (e.g. an <ol> closed by a stray </ul>, confirmed live to occur in real-world malformed source HTML) silently skipped the pop instead of performing it, permanently leaving the stack one level too deep for the rest of the document and bleeding a bogus off-by-one depth into every subsequent list, including completely unrelated, later, well-formed ones (#382). _resume_interrupted_block already handles the equivalent node-type correctness concern for this same malformed-tag scenario unconditionally (it's called for both <ol> and <ul> closes regardless of which opened the interrupted block); the fix applies the identical unconditional-pop principle to _list_ordered itself — any </ol> or </ul> means one fewer list is open, popped by count rather than gated on matching the popped entry's own type. Well-formed (correctly matched) nesting is unaffected, since the gate was already true in that case. _resume_interrupted_block itself had the same class of gap one level up (#450, surfaced during PR #449's QA pass on #382 and confirmed pre-existing, not a regression from that PR): it matched a _BlockFrame only by comparing its interrupted_by tag against the exact closing tag, so a mismatched <ol>/<ul> pair left the frame stuck on _block_stack rather than resolving it either way — a later, unrelated, well-formed list could then close with a tag that happened to match the stale frame's interrupted_by value, incorrectly restoring self._block_tag to the original (long-since-closed) outer block and mistyping subsequent bare trailing text as that stale block type. Fixed by giving _BlockFrame a list_depth field (the _list_ordered depth recorded at interrupt time, set only for list-category frames) and matching list interruptions by returning to that depth rather than by tag identity: the frame is always popped once the depth is reached, even on a mismatch, but the outer block is only actually resumed (self._block_tag restored) on an exact tag match — a mismatched close proves the interrupting list ended but never proves the outer block's own close tag was seen, so restoring it would be guessing. This requires _list_ordered's own unconditional pop (the #382 fix above) to run before _resume_interrupted_block for the same closing tag rather than after, since the depth check needs the post-pop count. PR #478's own review round caught a second, related bug in the same function, live-reproduced: bare top-level text directly inside a still-open <ol>/<ul> (not wrapped in its own <li>) opens an implicit paragraph via handle_data's bare-text path (#343) without going through _interrupt_open_block, so it has no frame of its own on _block_stack — resuming an outer interrupted frame while that implicit paragraph was still open unconditionally overwrote self._block_tag and cleared self._run_buf, silently destroying its text (<h1>Start<ol><li>B<ul><li>C</li></ol>D</ol>E dropped "D" entirely and mistyped "E" as a new heading instead of resuming "Start"'s own paragraph). Fixed by flushing whatever block is currently open, exactly the way _interrupt_open_block already does, before actually resuming — a no-op for every other call site into _resume_interrupted_block (table/pre/block-tag closes), since each of those already guarantees nothing is open at that point; only the list-close sites can reach it with something open. The same edit collapsed the function's two branches' duplicate self._block_stack.pop() call into one, per the same review round's non-blocking nit. The <pre> close-tag handler builds its Paragraph directly rather than going through _emit_block_node, so the #401/#402 fresh-vs-resumed whitespace distinction didn't automatically extend to it — a resumed <pre> (interrupted by a nested construct, e.g. a <table>) kept its trailing whitespace-only flush unconditionally, producing a spurious visible-space paragraph (#443). Fixed by applying the same fresh-vs-resumed check directly in the <pre> handler, while still keeping a fresh <pre>'s own whitespace unconditionally (every character inside <pre> is normally significant, unlike <p>); a resumed <pre> that dropped genuinely unsupported content (e.g. a <hr> inside <pre>) still gets a boundary node via the same preserve_if_empty guarantee every other block type gets, caught in PR #515's own QA round. <blockquote> (#476) plugs into the existing interrupt/resume machinery the same way <ol>/<ul>/<table>/<pre> already do — self._blockquote_depth increments/decrements on open/close, and _emit_block_node reads it directly when building each node's blockquote_depth field (a flat integer on Heading/Paragraph/BulletItem/NamedBlock, mirroring how BulletItem.depth encodes list nesting rather than a wrapper node — see docs/design/blockquote-representation.md for the representation decision and why a wrapper node was rejected). PR #546's own QA round 1 found two gaps: three Paragraph-construction sites (bare <hr>, bare <img>, <pre>'s own close handler) built their node directly rather than through _emit_block_node, so each silently defaulted to blockquote_depth=0 — fixed by passing blockquote_depth=self._blockquote_depth explicitly at each site. Separately, _resume_interrupted_block's PR #478 flush-before-resume step (described two sentences above) was only reachable from inside the "a frame exists and will be resumed" branch — a wrapper construct that opened with nothing outer to interrupt (so _interrupt_open_block pushed no frame at all) whose own inner content was left open at close time skipped the flush entirely, confirmed to reproduce identically for plain <ul>text</ul>after with no blockquote involved (a pre-existing gap in the shared mechanism, not something new to blockquote). Fixed by moving the flush to run unconditionally at the top of the function, before the if not self._block_stack: return check — closing the gap for every wrapper construct at once rather than patching blockquote's own manifestation of it.

docs.title: tools/docs/emitter.py
docs.text: docs/emitter.py — AST→Docs API requests + multi-phase table fill including nested table and cell styling support. ast_to_requests's BulletItem handling (#336) emits nesting level (BulletItem.depth, correctly computed by html_parser.py but previously never read here) as leading " " characters on each paragraph's own text — createParagraphBullets is the only Docs API mechanism for setting a bullet's nesting level, and it works by inferring each covered paragraph's level from, then consuming (removing), that paragraph's leading tab characters at the time the request executes. One call per contiguous same-preset run, not one call per paragraph — confirmed live (PR #432 QA round 1) that issuing a separate createParagraphBullets call per paragraph lets call order/adjacency to an already-bulleted neighbor override the tab-encoded depth: a live documents.get on the result showed sibling paragraphs at the identical AST depth landing under different listIds (each an independent, newly-created list) instead of one shared list with per-paragraph nestingLevel, and ordered lists lost continuous numbering as a result. The fix — confirmed correct via a live round-trip against the real API (shared listId, correct explicit nestingLevel per paragraph, continuous numbering) — groups maximal contiguous runs of same-ordered-value BulletItems (a preset change, e.g. an <ol> nested inside a <ul>, ends a run) into exactly one createParagraphBullets call spanning the whole run, so the API computes every paragraph's level from the tabs within that one call rather than relative to whatever's already rendered from a prior, separate call. A run with no depth-0 paragraph of its own (e.g. a preset-boundary child list, or issue #336's own "bare parent" case — a bare <li> holding only a nested <ul>, whose empty parent <li> html_parser.py drops) is "isolated": createParagraphBullets sets each covered paragraph's nestingLevel to (its leading-tab count) − (the minimum leading-tab count across the whole call's range), so with no 0-tab paragraph the entire run collapses to nestingLevel 0. The original #432 fix left the per-level indent bumped so such a run still looked one level deep, but it rendered the depth-0 glyph (● disc) instead of the correct nested glyph (○ circle at depth 1) — issue #439. Now fixed: an isolated run is wrapped with a throwaway 0-tab anchor paragraph — insertText " " at run_start, createParagraphBullets over the range extended by 1, then deleteContentRange the anchor — so the real items land at their true nestingLevel and its glyph (confirmed live, any depth: a min-depth-2 run resolves to nestingLevel 2). This is deliberate, not an accident of the anchor mechanic: because the anchor always contributes 0 tabs, nestingLevel for every item in an isolated run always equals its own depth exactly, with no clamp — a min_depth == 2 fragment (e.g. two levels of empty parent <li>s dropped, leaving only depth=2 children) renders two indent tiers deep with no visible parent above it. Issue #714 confirmed this is the intended behavior over clamping to depth 1: the converter renders the source's true structure faithfully rather than second-guessing a fragment whose ancestors were dropped only for having no text of their own. The anchor insert (+1) and delete (−1) cancel, so every position outside [run_start, run_end] — later bullet runs, the insertTable/image pass — is left exactly where an ordinary single createParagraphBullets call would leave it, and the descending-document-order application still holds (a lower run's net-zero anchor pair plus tab consumption never touches a higher, not-yet-processed run's range). Each bullet_run_requests entry is therefore a list of requests, not a single request. Because each grouped call still consumes tab characters (shifting every later document position backward by the run's total tab count), it can't run inline with the rest of the per-node request loop (which otherwise assumes no position ever shifts, true for every other request type) — it's deferred into a separate pass appended after all other per-node requests but before the insertTable pass, applied latest-document-position-first so consuming one run's tabs never invalidates the still-to-run range of an earlier, not-yet-processed run. insertTable positions are computed the same way they always were (as if the tabs were still present, since that's the coordinate space they were captured in while walking nodes) and then decremented by the cumulative tab count of every run positioned before that table, since by the time insertTable actually runs, all of those tabs have already been removed. A document with no nested (depth>0) bullets produces exactly the same one-call-per-contiguous-run shape it always would have, just now also merging what used to be separate same-preset flat-list calls into one — harmless, since a multi-paragraph call with zero tabs anywhere still assigns every paragraph level 0. Blockquote content (#476, any node with blockquote_depth > 0) gets one additional updateParagraphStyle request setting indentStart (36pt × depth) and borderLeft (a constant gray solid line) — the closest visual equivalent to a real blockquote the Docs API's ParagraphStyle exposes, since there's no native blockquote namedStyleType. borderLeft was live-verified writable via a scratch-doc round trip before implementing (per this file's own "Verify a ticket's API premise live" rule) rather than trusted from the discovery schema's silence on read-only status alone — the same class of field tabStops (#404) turned out NOT to be despite looking identical on paper. Issue #719: ast_to_requests used to join a code-block Paragraph's Run text (which legitimately contains embedded " " line breaks for a multi-line fenced block, per html_parser.py's <pre> handling) straight into the shared insertText call — but the Docs API treats every " " in inserted text as a new paragraph boundary regardless of styling, so a single multi-line code block silently fragmented into one NORMAL_TEXT Docs paragraph per line, contradicting markdown-support.md's own documented mapping of a fenced block to one "monospace paragraph" (confirmed live both ways: creation still applied Courier New to every fragment correctly, but get_doc_as_markdown's round-trip then re-rendered each fragment as its own tiny separate fence instead of one — reproducing identically for plain code content, not just HTML-tag content despite the issue's original title). Fixed via _is_code_paragraph (mirrors ast_to_markdown.py's _is_code_block, duplicated rather than imported to avoid a write/read circular import): a code-styled Paragraph's internal " " breaks are substituted with "\v" (the same soft-line-break convention insert_softbreak_paragraph already uses) before insertion, keeping the whole block one Docs paragraph while still rendering each line on its own visual line; the node's own trailing separator " " to the next AST node is untouched. doc_to_ast.py's _text_run_to_run reverses the substitution ("\v" → " ") for any run whose weightedFontFamily is Courier New specifically, so the reversal can't misinterpret an unrelated genuine soft break in non-code content — which currently has no reverse conversion of its own and round-trips as a literal "\v" character, a separate, pre-existing gap left out of scope here. Issue #434 (7 non-blocking findings from /code-review high on PR #432, never previously acted on) was resolved, across two PR #768 rounds, as: finding 1 fixed — a literal leading tab in a BulletItem's own source text (indistinguishable from the synthesized depth-tabs once concatenated) is stripped from its joined run text before combining with tabs, since left in place it both nests the item one level too deep and silently under-counts cumulative_tabs, desyncing any later table/image position (TC-DOC193); finding 3 fixed — an orphan <li> outside any <ul>/<ol> (node.depth would otherwise be -1) is clamped to a minimum of 0 at the actual source, html_parser.py::_make_bullet_item's depth = len(self._list_ordered) - 1, rather than by 3 separate downstream emitter.py call sites each independently remembering to — so it takes the same 1-request min_depth == 0 path a normal depth-0 item does instead of the 3-request isolated-wrap path purely because of an unclamped sign (TC-DOC194, unit-test-only; both converge on the identical rendered nestingLevel 0, so this is an efficiency/consistency fix with no observable output change); finding 4 fixed alongside 3 — the 3 now-redundant max(node.depth, 0) clamps in emitter.py were removed once the source-level clamp made them unreachable; findings 5+7 fixed — the three separately-appended parallel lists (tables/table_positions/table_tab_offsets) were consolidated into one pending_tables: list[_PendingTable] (a small local dataclass), and the previously-inlined table_positions[i] - table_tab_offsets[i] position correction is now a named position variable at its one call site, closing finding 7 as a byproduct; finding 6 fixed — ast_to_requests's docstring now documents all 3 ordering-sensitive request stages, and the previously-untyped positional segment_meta 5-tuple became a typed _SegmentMeta dataclass, mirroring _PendingTable's own rationale; finding 2 was already moot — the cited cumulative_tabs += len(tabs) never actually shipped that way (PR #432's own merged commit already used utf16_len(tabs), confirmed via git show); finding 4's original ask (generalizing the deferred-request mechanism into a reusable "this request consumes/shifts positions" abstraction, framed by its own filing as speculative future-proofing rather than a described defect) was deliberately left unimplemented, per this repo's standing guidance against designing for hypothetical future requirements — note this is a different "finding 4" than QA round 2's own locally-numbered findings, described next. PR #768's own QA round 1 (Kit) caught that the first version of finding 1's fix only stripped the leading tab from the concatenated run_text string used to build the inserted text, not the underlying Run/Image objects the per-run style/position offset loop iterates over afterward — a styled run's updateTextStyle range, and an Image's insertInlineImage position, both still counted via utf16_len(item.text) on the unstripped original text, overrunning by however many tab characters were actually stripped but never inserted (live-confirmed: a depth=0 BulletItem(runs=[Run(' Hello', bold=True)])'s own bold range came back {startIndex: 1, endIndex: 7} when "Hello" — the only text actually inserted — occupies indices 1-6). Fixed by extracting the strip into _strip_bullet_leading_tabs, a pure, non-mutating helper (returns a new Run/Image sequence via dataclasses.replace, never touching the caller's own AST objects — this function must stay side-effect-free on caller-owned input, unlike html_parser.py::_make_bullet_item's in-place runs[0].text = ... mutation, which is safe only because it always operates on a list it just built from its own fresh buffer) and threading that stripped sequence through as _SegmentMeta.runs, which the offset loop now walks instead of node.runs directly. The same QA round also flagged that the strip's own content-loss tradeoff (a genuinely-authored leading tab, not just hand-formatting whitespace, is silently dropped — unconditional on depth, since even a depth-0 item's own literal leading tab is still misread as a nesting signal relative to the rest of its createParagraphBullets call) had no test covering depth 0 specifically and no comment calling out that it is content loss, not just a reinterpretation; both addressed with an explicit callout in the strip's own comment and a dedicated depth=0 regression test.

docs.title: Async execution
docs.text:
Async execution (execute_in_thread + thread_http, in http_transport.py): every @tool()-registered function is async def, and _timed's wrapper is unconditionally async def wrapper(...): return await func(...) — so any new tool must be async def, even one with no Google API calls (see tools/cache.py's get_cache_ttl/set_cache_ttl/refresh_cache for an example with an empty await-free body; a plain def there raises TypeError at call time since awaiting a sync return value fails — test_server.py::TestAllToolsAreAsync guards against this recurring). Every .execute() call is wrapped await execute_in_thread(chain.execute, service) (http_transport.py, re-exported from auth.py for existing imports) — do not write asyncio.to_thread(chain.execute, http=thread_http(service)) directly: thread_http(service) as an eagerly-evaluated kwarg resolves on the event-loop thread before the worker thread starts, so concurrent calls end up sharing one transport across threads (a real, live-reproduced bug, fixed in #183's follow-up round — see the decision doc). execute_in_thread defers the thread_http() call into the thread itself via a lambda. thread_http() hands each worker thread its own AuthorizedHttp transport built from the shared credentials, since the lifespan-scoped sheets_service/drive_service/etc. objects each carry one httplib2 transport that isn't safe for concurrent use across threads. Six multi-call tools (sync_folder, get_multiple_sheet_data, get_multiple_spreadsheet_summary, import_csv_to_sheet, share_spreadsheet, share_file) parallelize their per-item work via asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) instead of looping serially. cache.py's SQLite I/O deliberately stays synchronous, not to_thread-wrapped — see the comment in cache.py::_open(); the module's two Google-API-calling helpers (get_modified_time, fetch_sheets) are async def and do use execute_in_thread for their own .execute() calls. _BaseCache.snapshot_epoch()/store(..., epoch=...) guard against a refresh_cache() call landing mid-fetch and having its invalidation silently overwritten — wired up for SheetStructureCache/SheetDataCache/DriveFolderCache (not DocContentCache/CalendarCache), and scoped per key: a store is skipped only if an invalidation covering its own key, <id>: prefix, or the whole namespace landed after its snapshot (TTL expiry doesn't count). Size-bounded caches (max_results/rows_to_fetch) share _BaseCache._get_sized/_store_sized rather than re-implementing the rows_fetched sufficiency check (#698). Full rationale: docs/decisions/decision-async-tool-execution.md. When unit-testing genuine cross-thread concurrency (not just correctness) with a threading.Barrier or similar, the block must live inside the mocked .execute() call, not .list()/.create()/etc. — those are evaluated eagerly on the event-loop thread while building the call chain, before execute_in_thread ever hands off to a worker thread, so blocking there freezes the single-threaded event loop instead of proving concurrency (see tests/drive/test_transfer.py::TestSyncFolderRecursive::test_recursive_sibling_subfolders_descend_concurrently). download_folder/sync_folder (#316/#319) added ctx.report_progress() calls from inside each item's own per-item coroutine so updates stream as concurrent transfers complete rather than arriving in one burst after the whole gather resolves — any future tool adding progress reporting to a gather-based batch (tracked for the remaining asyncio.gather tools in #355) must wrap that report_progress call in its own try/except: it's awaited after the item's real work already succeeded or failed, with no other guard around it, so a report_progress exception (e.g. a dropped client session) would otherwise propagate out, get caught by the outer gather(..., return_exceptions=True), and overwrite an already-successful result with a spurious failure — confirmed live and fixed in PR #351's review round.

The per-thread transport thread_http builds drifted from googleapiclient's build_http() on two settings until #1129 (PR #1198): with no socket timeout, a silently dead connection hung a create_doc_from_file call for 30 minutes, and with 308 still a redirect, every resumable upload over 100 MB raised RedirectMissingLocation. QA round 1 found that an HTTP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS past the platform's time_t failed every call, hence the one-day cap. See docs/decisions/decision-http-socket-timeout.md.

docs.title: Sheets API TextFormatRun.startIndex is also UTF-16 code units
docs.text: Sheets API TextFormatRun.startIndex is also UTF-16 code units (confirmed via the API reference, same gotcha class as the Docs API note above): update_cells (tools/sheets/data.py) accepts a rich-text cell as a list of {"text": str, "hyperlink": str | None} run dicts for partial (rich-text) hyperlinks within a single cell (issue #89) — _build_rich_text_cell computes each run's startIndex via _utf16_len (sheets/helpers.py, which delegates to docs/indices.py's utf16_len rather than duplicating its per-character logic), not len(), so a run following an astral-plane character (emoji, some CJK/math symbols) lands at the correct offset. A data array with no rich-text cells still goes through the original whole-range values().update() USER_ENTERED path unchanged. A data array that mixes plain and rich-text cells does not — an earlier version wrote the whole range via values().update() with rich-text positions blanked to "", relying on the second batchUpdate pass (the one that writes the rich-text updateCells requests) to overwrite those blanks back; if that second call failed, the blank was never restored and the rich-text cells' prior content was lost (live-confirmed via TC-W34 review, PR #380). The fixed version writes only the actual plain-cell positions via a per-cell values().batchUpdate() instead, so the two passes never touch each other's cells and a failure in one can't corrupt the other's data. Because they're now two independent API calls whenever both plain and rich-text cells are present, the tool returns {"values_update": ..., "rich_text_update": ...} in that case rather than silently dropping one result — only a call with just one kind of cell returns that single call's raw response.

docs.title: MCP resources
docs.text: MCP resources: Two resources are registered — server://auth-status (active auth method and Drive capability limits) and spreadsheet://{spreadsheet_id}/info (sheet list and grid properties). Under mcp v1, neither took a ctx argument the way tools do — both fetched it explicitly via mcp.get_context().request_context.lifespan_context (FastMCP had no get_lifespan_context() method, confirmed absent as far back as mcp==1.27.1, so calling that nonexistent method was never a regression from #350's SDK bump; it was a pre-existing bug invisible to unit tests since TestAuthStatusResource only exercised _auth_status_json() directly, never the resource function itself — fixed in #363). Under mcp v2 (mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer, since #175), get_context() no longer exists at all, and Context injection for a static (non-templated) resource like server://auth-status isn't supported by the framework (confirmed live against mcp==2.0.0 — the decorator raises ValueError outright). The two resources now use different mechanisms accordingly: get_spreadsheet_info is a template resource ({spreadsheet_id} in its URI), where v2 does support Context injection the same way tools already get it — it takes ctx: Context as an ordinary parameter and reads ctx.request_context.lifespan_context. get_auth_status is static, so it reads the process-wide auth.get_lifespan_context() singleton described above instead — see docs/decisions/decision-mcp-v2-resource-context-access.md for the full rationale.

docs.title: MCP restart
docs.text:
MCP restart: After docker compose restart mcp-gee-sweet, Claude Code does not automatically reconnect to the SSE server — you must restart Claude Code too to re-establish the connection. The same staleness applies to a team role's own stdio mcp-gee-sweet-<name> server (confirmed while fixing #336): it's a single long-running subprocess that imports this package's code once at session start, so editing .py files afterward does not get picked up by that already-running process — a live tool call (e.g. create_doc) made after a mid-session edit silently exercises the pre-edit code, which can look exactly like a real live-rendering bug (it reproduced one that had already been fixed on disk). uv run python3 -c "..." invocations in the same worktree are unaffected (fresh interpreter, fresh import each time) and are the reliable way to live-verify a same-session code change against the real API without restarting the whole session — reuse mcp_gee_sweet.auth._oauth_creds() plus googleapiclient.discovery.build(...) directly (the same construction spreadsheet_lifespan uses) to get a real docs/drive service in a throwaway script. This is also the only way to inspect fields no tool surfaces, like documents().get()'s raw paragraph.bullet/lists — what actually pinned down PR #432's live nesting behavior.

The fresh interpreter is a workaround for the server's stale import, so it applies only to code the branch changed. While verifying PR #1089 (#1056), Jay found loose Markdown lists losing their bullets in html_parser.py, which that branch didn't touch, and filed #1111 on evidence from a script that applied _to_doc_requests' output directly. The ticket first claimed it was seen "through write_doc_content", then was reworded to describe the script instead of running the tool. The maintainer asked why it wasn't done live. write_doc_content plus get_doc_structure on the role's own server (which runs develop's parser) reproduced it in two calls, and #1111 was updated with that evidence.

docs.title: Regression vs. pre-existing bug after a dependency bump
docs.text: Regression vs. pre-existing bug after a dependency bump: when a bug report asks "is this a regression from the recent SDK bump" (e.g. issue #363 against #350's mcp>=1.28.1 change), don't answer from memory or by reading changelogs alone — install the old pinned version in a scratch venv and check the specific API surface directly against it (e.g. python3 -m venv /tmp/x && ./x/bin/pip install "mcp==1.27.1" && ./x/bin/python -c "from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP; print(hasattr(FastMCP, 'get_lifespan_context'))"). Confirmed in #363: FastMCP.get_lifespan_context() looked like it could've been removed by the bump, but it never existed even at 1.27.1 — the scratch-venv check settled the question in seconds instead of guessing from a diff.

docs.title: Verify a ticket's API premise live before implementing, not after
docs.text: Verify a ticket's API premise live before implementing, not after. An issue's ask can rest on an unverified assumption that a specific Google API field or request is settable, just because that field appears in the API's discovery schema — a schema documents read-only fields as ordinary properties, so presence alone doesn't mean writable. Before building a feature around a Google API capability not already confirmed live elsewhere in this codebase, run the same scratch-script check described above under "MCP restart" (uv run python3 -c "..." with mcp_gee_sweet.auth._oauth_creds() + googleapiclient.discovery.build(...)) against the live discovery document first — read the target field's own description for a "read-only" note, and confirm at least one request type in the schema actually references it for writing — before writing any implementation. Confirmed the hard way on issue #404/PR #471: style_doc_range shipped a full tab_stops implementation, unit tests, and QA test cases before QA's live round hit HttpError 400 ... "Unallowed field: tabStops". A follow-up discovery-schema check took two minutes and confirmed ParagraphStyle.tabStops's own description reads "This property is read-only," with no request type anywhere in the Docs API able to set it — the same check, run before implementation instead of after QA sent it back, would have caught this without costing a full dev+QA cycle. Closed as infeasible rather than fixed (issue #404, PR #471, follow-up #473 filed for the documented workaround).

docs.title: Procedural feedback → the governing command file, not memory
docs.text: Procedural feedback → the governing command file, not memory. If the human's feedback corrects or refines a repeatable team-workflow step that a .claude/team-roles/*.md or .claude/commands/*.md file already governs (or should) — as opposed to project context, an external-system pointer, or a one-off judgment call specific to the current conversation — that's a command decision (.claude/commands/retro.md's disposition), not a memory entry: edit the file directly, through Bob's prompt-QA gate (.claude/team-roles/bob.md), rather than trusting memory to carry it. A memory-only fix is retrieved heuristically and competes with whatever the loaded prompt already says instead of reliably overriding it — confirmed the hard way on PR #456: two separate memory-only fixes for QA's /mcp reconnect+/code-review batching (qa.md step 2) each got silently re-broken by a later session before the rule was hard-coded into qa-kickoff.md instead. Memory is still the right home for what's genuinely outside the team's tracked process — it just isn't a substitute for a rule a command file is meant to enforce every time.

docs.title: Re-authorizing OAuth from the Failing Tool Call
docs.text: Issue: #873 (folds in #906) · Date: 2026-10-06 · Status: implemented

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Before this change, an OAuth server with no usable token stayed broken until someone ran a terminal command and restarted it:

  • Degraded start (#811). With no usable token at startup, a stdio server starts without Google access. Every tool returned "run mcp-gee-sweet auth, then restart the server or reconnect".
  • Mid-session refresh failure. The token was revoked or expired after a good start. #811 didn't cover this. PR #905 added a re-authorize hint in _timed, but most tools catch the RefreshError in their own except Exception and return {"error": ...} before _timed sees it (#906). So list_files showed a raw tuple repr with no hint, while list_sheets, which lets the error propagate, showed the hint.

The goal is to recover in place, without the server opening a browser unprompted (one of #811's complaints), and without the model having to know about a separate tool.

docs.title: Client support (checked first, as the issue asked)
docs.text:
A probe server logged the initialize capabilities of Claude Code 2.1.291 as {"elicitation": {"form": {}, "url": {}}, "roots": {...}}, protocol 2026-07-28. So URL-mode elicitation is the main path, and the ToolError text is the fallback for other clients.

Under claude -p (no human), a tool raising UrlElicitationRequiredError came back to the model as "URL elicitation was canceled by the user". A headless client never shows the link. That's the client's behavior, and the CLI alternative still covers it.

docs.title: Mechanism: UrlElicitationRequiredError, not an in-call ctx.elicit_url
docs.text:
The tool call raises UrlElicitationRequiredError (JSON-RPC -32042). mcp's Tool.run re-raises an MCPError as a protocol error instead of wrapping it as a tool result.

The in-call alternative, ctx.elicit_url(), sends a server-to-client request and keeps the call open while the user decides. It would hold the call for up to OAUTH_CONSENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, and it needs a back-channel, which a 2026-07-28 request context may lack (NoBackChannelError). The error form returns immediately, and the consent runs on independently of any call.

When the consent completes, the server sends notifications/elicitation/complete to every session it offered the URL to. This is best effort: a gone session or a missing channel is logged at debug level and ignored.

docs.title: Noticing a rejected refresh in every tool
docs.text:
The issue comment pointed at execute_in_thread as the single choke point. It isn't quite one: media downloads (MediaIoBaseDownload.next_chunk) set request.http = thread_http(service) and never go through execute_in_thread. Every Google request does go through thread_http's transport, so that's where the hook sits. _RefreshTrackingHttp (an AuthorizedHttp subclass) records a non-retryable RefreshError on a per-call CallAuthState before re-raising it.

_timed opens the state with track_refresh_failures(), a ContextVar holding a mutable object. Gathered tasks and asyncio.to_thread workers copy the context, and the copy points at the same object, so a failure on any of them is seen. After the tool body returns or raises, a recorded failure replaces whatever the tool produced (including an {"error": ...} dict) with the re-authorization offer. The 86 tool-level except blocks stay untouched.

A retryable RefreshError (the token endpoint's own 5xx) isn't recorded: it says nothing about the token.

docs.title: Recovery order (reauth.py)
docs.text:
Both entry points, before_call (degraded connection) and after_refresh_failure (mid-session), try in order:

  1. Adopt a token this process already got. publish_oauth_credentials bumps a process-wide generation. A context built from an older generation rebuilds its services in place (apply_oauth_credentials) on its next call. One TOKEN_PATH means one token for every connection.
  2. Reload TOKEN_PATH (load_saved_token, on a daemon thread like the rest of the auth code). This picks up a token mcp-gee-sweet auth wrote, so the CLI no longer needs a restart. In the mid-session case a reloaded token with the same refresh token as the failing one is rejected: it's the same revoked grant. Two guards (PR #925 QA round 1):
  3. The reload doesn't touch the Gmail gate. It runs _oauth_creds(record_gmail=False), so the process-wide _gmail_unauthorized_message isn't reset and re-set by every connection's reload, whether or not anything gets adopted. publish_oauth_credentials sets the gate from the token actually adopted.
  4. An unchanged file isn't reloaded again. After a reload finds nothing to adopt, TOKEN_PATH's (mtime_ns, size) is remembered, and the reload is skipped until the file changes. Without this, a revoked token on disk cost a failing refresh round-trip and a warning on every call. mcp-gee-sweet auth rewrites the file, so it's still picked up.
  5. Offer consent. Start or join the shared listener and raise the elicitation, or the ToolError with the URL. The offer states the time the link actually has left (_ConsentAttempt.remaining_seconds), not the full timeout. A tool call's own attempt with less than min(60, timeout/2) seconds left is replaced by a fresh one rather than handed out. The replaced attempt isn't stopped: a client already holds its link, and its offer promised that link until its deadline. In PR #925's second round it was stopped, and QA reproduced a link dying with 7.9s of its stated time left. So two listeners can overlap, for at most min(60, timeout/2) seconds. The two attempts share a group, and whichever completes publishes the token and sends elicitation/complete to both attempts' clients.

When a degraded connection adopts a token, the tool body then runs normally. When a mid-session failure adopts one, the call ends with "a newer token was loaded; retry the call". The tool isn't re-run automatically, because a multi-request tool may already have made changes before the refresh failed. So the offer carries what the tool itself reported (describe_outcome, truncated at 1,500 characters): "The call may have partly completed before the token was rejected; the tool reported: ...". The model then knows what may already have happened.

docs.title: One listener per process, shared with the lifespan
docs.text:
start_user_consent reuses _consent_attempt, the slot #833 made process-wide. So a tool call that arrives during an SSE lifespan consent offers that consent's URL (_serve_consent's new on_url callback records it), and marks it offered: once a client holds the link, the last lifespan waiter leaving no longer stops the attempt and closes its port. _ConsentListener splits binding the callback server and building the URL from the wait, so the URL exists before anything blocks. The build runs on a daemon thread. If the call is cancelled during it, a done callback closes the listener once it's bound. That's a callback rather than an await in cleanup, so a cancel scope's re-delivered cancellation can't skip it.

The reverse doesn't join. A lifespan that needs consent while a tool call's attempt is pending doesn't wait on it: nothing would be shown to anyone for that wait. It starts without access at once, raising OAuthConsentRequiredError(disables_consent=False) so degrading doesn't turn consent off, and the connection's first tool call offers the same link. In PR #925's first round the lifespan did join. QA reproduced the result over SSE: a connection waited out the whole timeout with no prompt, then turned server consent off for every later connection.

A tool call's attempt (user_started) differs from a lifespan's in three ways:

  • It never opens a browser and prints no stderr prompt; the client shows the URL.
  • No waiter's departure stops it, since the call that started it has already returned. It runs to its timeout.
  • Its failure doesn't turn off _interactive_consent.

docs.title: Restart wording
docs.text:
reauthorize_instructions(restart=False) ends "then retry the call: the server picks up the new token without a restart". It's used everywhere the token is missing or rejected: the degraded-start messages, server://auth-status, and the offer's CLI alternative. mcp-gee-sweet auth prints the same. Only the missing-scope messages (#790, including Gmail's) still say to restart, since nothing reloads the token there.

_client_error keeps its re-authorize hint for a non-retryable RefreshError that reaches it without going through the offer. A retryable one (the token endpoint's own 5xx) gets no hint, and it is reported as a plain error.

docs.title: The issue's open questions
docs.text:
• SSE's "consent is never retried" rule. It still governs the server's own consent in the lifespan, which an unattended server shouldn't keep restarting for every connection. A tool-call consent is started by a user, from a client, one at a time. Its failure only means the next failing call offers a fresh URL. start_user_consent deliberately ignores _interactive_consent, which is also what lets it run under stdio.
  • mcp-gee-sweet auth's role. It becomes the secondary path. It's still documented in docs/auth.md and still named in every offer, for clients that can't show the link. It's still the only fix for a missing-scope token (below).

docs.title: thread_http cache
docs.text: Rebuilding the services makes new service objects, and CPython can reuse a freed object's id(). The per-thread transport cache was keyed on id(service) alone, so a rebuilt service could get a stale transport holding the revoked credentials. A cached transport is now reused only while http.credentials is service._http.credentials.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Missing scopes aren't offered. A token lacking a base scope still stops a stdio server at startup (#790), and a Gmail-only shortfall still degrades only the Gmail tools. Both still need mcp-gee-sweet auth and a restart.
  • The callback listens on localhost. The browser that completes the consent must run on the server's machine. This already applied to the lifespan's own SSE consent; it matters more now that a remote SSE client can be shown the link.
  • A headless client cancels the elicitation. The user never sees the link (see above).

docs.title: Design: Phase 3 — Theme System (get_doc_theme / apply_theme)
docs.text:
Date: 2026-06-20 Issue: #88 Status: complete

Point-in-time implementation design — captures the key discovery, data model, and approach decisions. See docs-ast-pipeline.md for Phase 2 context.

docs.title: What Phase 3 adds
docs.text:
1. Emitter Phase 3 Run fields — activates the Run.font_size, Run.foreground_color, Run.background_color, Run.baseline_offset, Run.small_caps AST stubs in _run_style_requests (previously silently ignored).

  2. Emitter Cell styling (Step 7) — new _build_cell_style_requests helper; fill_tables now emits updateTableCellStyle for cells with background_color, padding_*, or border_* fields set.

  3. get_doc_theme tool — scans body.content paragraphs and returns a theme dict keyed by named style type, reading the first paragraph per type as representative. Text-level fields come from the first non-empty text run; paragraph-level fields come from paragraphStyle. Only works for docs with explicit per-paragraph styles (AI-generated content); returns empty for docs whose styles are purely inherited from named style defaults.

  4. apply_theme tool — applies a theme dict by emitting updateNamedStyle requests (one per named style key) to update the document's named style definitions. An overwrite=True param additionally applies styles directly to all existing paragraphs via updateParagraphStyle / updateTextStyle. Also handles a "table" key via updateTableCellStyle.

docs.title: Key API discovery: updateNamedStyle (singular) works
docs.text:
The original implementation tried updateNamedStyles (plural), which returned HTTP 400 ("Unknown name"). The correct batchUpdate request type is updateNamedStyle (singular, camelCase). Confirmed via the Docs API discovery doc (UpdateNamedStyleRequest schema).

Field mask requirements (discovered during live QA): - Paths are snake_case (text_style.bold, paragraph_style.line_spacing) — not camelCase - named_style_type must always be included in the field mask, or the API returns HTTP 400 "Named style type is required" - The root named_style prefix is implied and must not appear in the mask

get_doc_theme originally read from doc.namedStyles.styles (the document's named style template defaults). This works for standard Google Docs but returns empty for AI-generated docs, which store styles as explicit per-paragraph and per-run overrides and leave namedStyles at Google's blank defaults. The implementation was replaced with a body paragraph scan.

docs.title: Chosen approach: updateNamedStyle + optional paragraph overwrite
docs.text:
apply_theme (default mode):

  1. For each named style key in the theme, emits one updateNamedStyle request
  2. Updates the document's named style definitions — affects all future paragraphs that inherit from those named styles
  3. Does not fetch the doc or touch existing paragraphs; existing explicit overrides are unaffected
  4. For the optional "table" key, fetches the doc and emits updateTableCellStyle rows per table

apply_theme with overwrite=True:

  1. Same updateNamedStyle requests as above
  2. Additionally fetches the full doc and scans body.content
  3. For each paragraph matching a named style key, emits updateParagraphStyle / updateTextStyle
  4. This overwrites any existing per-paragraph style overrides

Trade-off (default mode): Named style updates affect new paragraphs but may not visually change existing content if those paragraphs have explicit overrides (the override wins). Use overwrite=True to force-apply to all existing paragraphs.

Trade-off (get_doc_theme body scan): Only returns data for docs where styles are stored as explicit paragraph/run overrides. For standard docs with inherited styles, returns empty. Combine with overwrite=True in an AI-generated-doc workflow where you know styles are explicit.

docs.title: Theme dict schema
docs.text:
{
    # Named style type key → style entry (all fields optional)
    "HEADING_1": {
        "font_family": "Georgia",  # str
        "font_size": 20.0,  # float, points
        "bold": True,  # bool
        "italic": False,  # bool
        "color": {"red": 0, "green": 0, "blue": 0},  # RGB 0-1
        "line_spacing": 115,  # float, 100=single
        "space_above": 12.0,  # float, points
        "space_below": 6.0,  # float, points
    },
    "NORMAL_TEXT": {...},
    # Optional: apply default cell styling to all tables in the doc
    "table": {
        "border_color": {"red": 0, "green": 0, "blue": 0},
        "border_width": 0.5,  # float, points
        "border_dash_style": "SOLID",  # str
        "cell_padding": 3.6,  # float, points (all four sides)
        "header_background": {"red": 0.953, "green": 0.953, "blue": 0.953},  # first row only
    },
}

Valid named style type keys: NORMAL_TEXT, HEADING_1–HEADING_6, TITLE, SUBTITLE.

docs.title: Named theme management (deferred)
docs.text: Storing and re-using named themes (e.g. "corporate", "report") was explicitly deferred. The current design is inline-only: the caller passes the theme dict directly. A future spike (#TBD) should design the storage layer, covering all server config variants (Docker volume, local process, service account without persistent filesystem, ADC).

docs.title: SSE OAuth Consent Off the Event Loop
docs.text: Date: 2026-10-01 · Issue: #833 (follow-up to #811 / PR #828) · Module: src/mcp_gee_sweet/auth.py

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Under --transport sse with no usable OAuth token, the lifespan ran the browser consent (InstalledAppFlow.run_local_server) directly on the event loop. Until the user consented or OAUTH_CONSENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS passed:

  • every other request stalled, because the loop was blocked
  • SIGTERM didn't stop the server. Uvicorn's shutdown waits for open connections, and the connection holding the consent couldn't finish until its lifespan did. QA had to SIGKILL it (TC-I38, TC-I40).

docs.title: 1. The lifespan awaits a daemon thread
docs.text:
_oauth_creds(defer_consent=True) does everything up to the consent (token load, refresh), then raises _ConsentDeferred instead of running it. _oauth_creds_async() (what the lifespan calls) runs that on a daemon thread (oauth-token), so a hanging token endpoint can't block the loop either (PR #867 QA round 1). On _ConsentDeferred it awaits _await_server_consent(), which runs the flow on a thread named oauth-consent. Both go through _run_in_daemon_thread and _await_unless_shutdown (§4).

These are daemon threads, not asyncio.to_thread. Interpreter shutdown joins the default executor's worker threads, so a consent still waiting there would hold process exit until the timeout. The hang would just move from the event loop to shutdown (Kai's triage note on #833).

The sync _oauth_creds() (no flag) still runs the consent inline. Only scratch scripts use it that way; the server never does.

docs.title: 2. Our own callback server instead of run_local_server
docs.text:
_serve_consent() replaces the library's run_local_server for the server's consent. It does the same steps: a wsgiref server on a random localhost port, flow.authorization_url(), open the browser, take the first request, flow.fetch_token(). It changes two things:

  • Stoppable. The library makes one blocking handle_request() call for the whole timeout, so nothing outside the call can end it early. Ours calls handle_request() with a 0.5s timeout in a loop, checking the deadline and a threading.Event.
  • Prompt on stderr without redirect_stdout. The library print()s its prompt to stdout, and #811 moved it with redirect_stdout(sys.stderr). That swaps sys.stdout for every thread in the process, which was harmless only while nothing else could run. We print(..., file=sys.stderr) ourselves.

The same first-request semantics are kept: a stray request ends the wait, and fails on the state check (TC-I40 run 2). The request handler has a 5s socket timeout: a connection that sends nothing (a browser preconnect, a port scanner) would otherwise block handle_request() in readline() with no deadline or stop check (PR #867 QA round 1). The dropped connection is logged at debug, not as a traceback. A missing browser (webbrowser.Error, e.g. in a container) no longer fails the flow; the URL is on stderr regardless. The request handler logs nothing, since the request line carries the authorization code. mcp-gee-sweet auth keeps using the library's run_local_server, because a terminal is where its stdout prompt belongs.

docs.title: 3. One shared attempt
docs.text:
_consent_attempt is process-wide on purpose. A connection that opens while a consent is in flight awaits the same future (one prompt, one callback port) instead of starting a second consent. Each waiter awaits it through asyncio.shield, so cancelling one connection doesn't cancel the attempt for the others. When the last waiter is cancelled, the stop event is set. The thread then exits within one poll and closes the port. That kind of cancellation isn't a failed attempt, so _interactive_consent stays on.

The "no retry after a failed attempt" rule from #811 is unchanged, but its reason has changed. The wait no longer blocks the server. Retrying would make an unattended server print a new prompt and hold each new connection for the timeout.

Consent is turned off when the attempt settles with an error, on the loop, before any waiter sees the failure (_ConsentAttempt._on_settle), not later in the lifespan. Two reasons (PR #867 QA round 1). A waterfall that falls back to a service account never reaches _degrade_unauthorized, so the next connection prompted again. And with the lifespan doing it, a connection opening in the few loop hops between the future failing and the lifespan degrading saw a settled attempt with consent still on, and started another.

The token load runs on its own thread, so a connection can decide "consent needed" and reach the loop after an attempt has settled (PR #867 CI flake and QA round 4). Both outcomes are handled on the loop: after a failure, _await_server_consent re-checks _interactive_consent before starting an attempt. After a success, a counter (_consent_successes, bumped in _on_settle) tells _oauth_creds_async that a consent finished while its load ran, and it reads the token again instead of starting a second consent. It doesn't reuse the finished attempt's credentials, because a connection whose load starts after a success and still finds no usable token (say, the token was deleted to re-authorize) should get a new consent, not the old credentials.

docs.title: 4. Noticing shutdown
docs.text: The lifespan runs inside the SSE request, and nothing cancels it on SIGTERM: sse_starlette ends the response stream, but connect_sse's task group still waits for the body (the lifespan). So _await_unless_shutdown polls sse_starlette.sse.AppStatus.should_exit alongside the future. That flag is sse_starlette's public shutdown signal, set from uvicorn's exit handler, and it's how SSE streams learn to close. When it flips, the waiter raises OAuthConsentRequiredError("...the server shut down before the browser consent completed..."). The lifespan then degrades normally, the connection finishes, and uvicorn exits. The consent thread is stopped the same way as for a cancellation.

docs.title: 5. Auth failures degrade outside stdio
docs.text:
Moving the token load off the loop changed when a failing lifespan raises: after its first await, so after the SSE response task has already sent the endpoint event. A client that POSTs initialize the instant it sees that event gets 202, and the POST then waits in writer.send() on mcp's zero-buffer session stream. Server.run never starts reading it, and connect_sse never closes it when the body raises, so the POST waits forever and SIGTERM hangs on it (Waiting for background tasks to complete). On develop the lifespan raised before any await, before the endpoint event went out, so no client could POST. PR #867 QA round 2 hit this 3 times in 39; a client that POSTs immediately hits it every time (25 of 25). It reproduces on a bare mcp 2.0.0 server with no code of ours, filed upstream as python-sdk#3616 (related: python-sdk#514).

The fix is in our lifespan, not mcp's transport: spreadsheet_lifespan wraps _build_context(), and outside stdio any exception becomes a degraded connection (_degraded_context) whose unauthorized_message is the failure (with its cause). The connection then runs normally, so a raced-in POST is read. Raising bought nothing over SSE anyway: the server keeps running, and the client only saw "Connection closed". Now every tool call returns the actual reason, such as the missing-scopes re-authorize instructions. server.main() sets set_raise_auth_failures(True) for stdio, which keeps #790's fail-fast exit there; stdio has no POST endpoint, so no race. #790's other rule is unchanged: a token on disk missing scopes still isn't masked by falling through to a service account.

Patching mcp's transport instead was rejected: it means carrying a copy of connect_sse (or monkeypatching it), which silently goes stale on mcp upgrades, for a transport the MCP spec has deprecated.

docs.title: Verified live (2026-10-01, dummy installed-app client JSON, BROWSER=/usr/bin/true)
docs.text:
develop before this change POST /messages/ during the wait no answer within 5s 400 in 0.07s SIGTERM during the wait still running after 15s exited in 0.39s, both ports released A, then B during the wait (timeout 4s) n/a 1 prompt, both degrade "within 4s"; C afterward degrades with no wait Stray callback request degrades in 0.08s (MismatchingStateError) Missing-scope token, client POSTs initialize on the endpoint event, then SIGTERM n/a (no endpoint before the raise) before §5: 25 of 25 hang. After: 0 of 25, POST 202; a real sse_client initializes and gets the missing-scopes message as the tool error

An Exception in ASGI application ... Expected ASGI message 'http.response.body' traceback at shutdown appeared on develop too, for any SSE stream open at SIGTERM, so it was unrelated to this change. #868 fixed it with SingleResponseGuard (sse_shutdown.py).

docs.title: Not changed
docs.text: The synchronous _oauth_creds() (no flag) still runs everything inline, for scratch scripts. _server_shutting_down reads only AppStatus.should_exit, not sse_starlette's fallback that introspects uvicorn's signal handler: its monkey-patch works in our launch path (TC-I43).

docs.title: QA Workflow
docs.text: Prompt-driven integration tests for mcp-gee-sweet. Each test case is a natural language prompt you issue to Claude via the MCP server, paired with a list of things to verify in the response.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A running mcp-gee-sweet server (Docker or uv run mcp-gee-sweet)
  • Auth configured (service account or OAuth) with access to your Google Drive
  • Claude Desktop or Claude Code connected to the server

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Set up fixtures — follow setup.md to create your test spreadsheet, doc, and calendar fixtures. Takes about 5 minutes.
  2. Record your IDs — copy fixtures.template.md → fixtures.local.md (gitignored) and fill in the IDs from step 1.
  3. Run tests — paste the conductor prompt from run.md into a Claude session that has both the mcp-gee-sweet MCP server and the Playwright MCP connected. Claude will execute the tests, visually verify mutations in the browser via Playwright, and save a report to results/.
  4. Review the report — check results/<date>.md for failures and the tool coverage checklist (lists every tool, which TCs exercise it, and which tools have no coverage at all).
  5. Report failures — open a GitHub issue with the TC number, the exact prompt used, what was observed, and what Playwright showed.

docs.title: Release runs
docs.text: runs/ contains one file per stable release (vX.Y.Z.md). Each file is the sign-off record for that release — a checklist of required suites, links to result files, and a final sign-off. A completed run file is required before tagging any stable release. See runs/README.md for suite tier definitions (smoke / domain / full regression).

docs.title: Test files
docs.text: File Category TC prefix tests/sheets_read.md Sheets read tools TC-R## tests/sheets_write.md Sheets write tools TC-W## tests/sheets_mgmt.md Sheets management tools TC-S## tests/sheets_charts.md Sheets chart tools TC-C## tests/drive_files.md Drive files & folders TC-D## tests/drive_sharing.md Drive sharing & permissions TC-D## tests/drive_transfer.md Drive upload/download/sync/export/revisions TC-D## tests/drive_activity.md Drive activity TC-D## tests/docs_content.md Docs content — content.py plus the catch-all for editing.py/images.py/comments.py/named_ranges.py and the markdown/HTML conversion pipeline (unlike the other 7 files, not a 1:1 submodule mapping — see the file's own Source line) TC-DOC## (plus TC-D## carried over from create_doc/get_doc_content/write_doc_content cases originally numbered under drive.md) tests/docs_tables.md Docs tables TC-DOC## tests/docs_style.md Docs style & theming TC-DOC## tests/docs_layout.md Docs layout (headers/footers) TC-DOC## tests/docs_markdown.md Markdown → Docs rendering through every write path; the v0.9.3 release gate (#1044) TC-MD### tests/infra.md Infrastructure TC-I## tests/calendar.md Calendar tools TC-CAL## tests/gmail.md Gmail tools TC-GM##

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Tests marked ⚠️ destructive mutate the fixture spreadsheet. Run these last within their section or reset fixtures afterward using the seed prompt in setup.md.
  • Tests marked ⚠️ requires-oauth need OAuth or ADC auth — service accounts cannot create or copy files in Drive (no storage quota). These tests are automatically skipped with a warning when QA_AUTH_METHOD=service_account in .env.
  • Tests marked ⚠️ local-filesystem need file paths accessible to the MCP server process. A full conductor run skips them. A scoped lane pass can still run the ones that test server startup or a CLI subcommand (auth waterfall, stdio/SSE behavior, mcp-gee-sweet auth) by starting its own server process; see run.md §"Running server-startup and CLI cases in a scoped lane pass". A representative subset is instead covered by the opt-in tests/integration/ pytest harness (MCP_GEE_SWEET_LIVE_TESTS=1 uv run python -m pytest tests/integration/ — needs real Google credentials, see that package's conftest.py) — see decision-local-fs-test-harness.md for what it covers and what's still follow-up.
  • Tests marked 🔍 product decision have no single correct answer — note what you observed and open an issue if the behavior seems wrong.
  • Cache hit tests (TC-R17, TC-S02, etc.) require checking server logs: make logs or docker compose logs mcp-gee-sweet.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: If you find a bug or surprising behavior, open a GitHub issue. To add a new test case, submit a PR adding it to the relevant file in tests/ with the next sequential TC number.

docs.title: Test case format
docs.text:
Each test case follows this structure:

### TC-XNN: Short description [tags]

**Setup:** <precondition — fixture file path or live doc state to establish>

**Prompt**
> "Natural language instruction to Claude"

**Checks**
- Specific key or value to verify in the response (e.g. "`docId` returned with no `error`")
- Structural assertion (e.g. "`get_doc_structure` shows HEADING_1 "Foo" and a table")
- 🔍 Visual check: anything that requires opening the doc/sheet in a browser

**Cleanup:** what to delete or tear down

**Result:** ⏳ pending  ← replaced with date + PASS/FAIL after live run

docs.title: Fixture files
docs.text: If a test needs a local file (e.g. a .md or .html to upload), commit it to docs/qa/fixtures/ and reference it by repo path — don't ask the tester to write content by hand. Name fixtures after their TC number: tc-d195-create-doc.md. Note: several docs.md fixtures (tc-d195-*, tc-d196-*, tc-d213-*, tc-d226-*) still carry TC-D##-prefixed filenames from before docs.md was split onto its own TC-DOC## sequence — their current headers are TC-DOC44, TC-DOC45, etc., not the number in the filename. Don't assume a TC-D<N>-shaped filename means that number is claimed in drive.md's own sequence, and don't assume a fixture's filename number matches its test case's current number.

docs.title: Checks quality bar
docs.text:
• Name specific keys, values, or text strings — not vague descriptions like "the response looks right"
  • Visual checks (🔍) are fine for things the API doesn't surface (e.g. rendered font size in Google Docs)
  • Error-path tests should name the exact error key or message fragment expected

docs.title: Fixtures
docs.text:
Fixture IDs now live in .env at the repo root (gitignored), not in this file.

Copy the block below into your .env and fill in your IDs after running the seed prompt in setup.md.

# Server default create-location — the mcp-gee-sweet-shared Shared Drive ID
DRIVE_FOLDER_ID=          # same value as SHARED_DRIVE_ID below

# QA test fixtures (provisioned inside the mcp-gee-sweet-shared Shared Drive)
TEST_SPREADSHEET_ID=       # mcp-gee-sweet-qa-fixtures spreadsheet
TEST_DOC_ID=               # mcp-gee-sweet-qa-fixtures-doc
TEST_FOLDER_ID=            # the Shared Drive folder containing the fixture files
TEST_LARGE_DOC_ID=         # mcp-gee-sweet-qa-large-doc (TC-D48 large-content test)
TEST_CALENDAR_ID=          # a calendar the authenticated account can access
TEST_EVENT_ID=             # a pre-existing event in that calendar
TEST_PERMISSION_EMAIL=     # a second account to use for permission add/remove tests (TC-D130)
SHARED_DRIVE_ID=           # mcp-gee-sweet-shared Shared Drive (TC-D121/D122/D205); = DRIVE_FOLDER_ID

# Gmail QA fixtures (written by scripts/qa_gmail_fixtures.py; see setup.md)
TEST_GMAIL_ADDRESS=        # QA mailbox (the OAuth fixture account)
TEST_GMAIL_SENDER_ADDRESS= # sender mailbox that delivers the sent fixtures
TEST_GMAIL_LABEL_ID=       # mcp-qa-fixture user label
TEST_MESSAGE_ID=           # plain
TEST_THREAD_ID=            # thread (3-message, two-party)
TEST_GMAIL_UNICODE_ID=     # alt-unicode
TEST_GMAIL_ATTACH_ID=      # attachments (PDF + CSV)
TEST_GMAIL_INLINE_ID=      # inline (multipart/related PNG, no filename)
TEST_GMAIL_REPLYTO_ID=     # reply-to (TC-GM23)
TEST_GMAIL_FWD_ID=         # forwarded (message/rfc822)
TEST_GMAIL_LARGE_ID=       # large-body (~3 MB, #803 item 2)
TEST_GMAIL_BIG_THREAD_ID=  # over-cap-thread
TEST_GMAIL_LATIN1_ID=      # latin1 (#792)

See setup.md for how to create the fixtures and which auth options require extra sharing steps.

docs.title: Gmail — QA Test Plan
docs.text:
Status: draft (2026-09-26), scoped under #803 Source under test: src/mcp_gee_sweet/tools/gmail.py Case file: tests/gmail.md (TC-GM01–45. TC-GM26 is the #792 charset case, so the §4.2 cases start at 27.)

This is the plan of record for testing the Gmail domain: what the mailbox fixture looks like, which behaviors need live coverage, and which gaps are tooling or product gaps rather than test gaps.

docs.title: 1. Where coverage stands today
docs.text:
Layer State Unit (tests/test_gmail.py, 59 tests) Strong on _reply_recipients (#791: 20 cases). Thin on MIME building and payload parsing (see §5). Live — reply routing (TC-GM23–25) ✅ Run 2026-09-26 on PR #815, both rounds. Live — everything else (TC-GM01–22) ❌ Never run. No **Result** exists in tests/gmail.md, results/, or runs/. #786 merged with unit tests only. Live — auth degradation (TC-I31–34, infra.md) ✅ Run on #790. Smoke suite (runs/README.md) ❌ No Gmail entry. A shared-layer regression that breaks Gmail passes Smoke. Fixtures (setup.md, fixtures.template.md) ❌ No Gmail section. operations.yaml names TEST_MESSAGE_ID/TEST_THREAD_ID but nothing creates them.

TC-GM01–22 also predate the prescriptive-case rule: most are one-line natural-language prompts ("List my 5 most recent inbox messages") with no exact tool name or params, and read against whatever happens to be in the inbox. They need rewriting against the fixture set below. TC-GM23–25 are the reference style.

docs.title: 2. Testability constraints
docs.text:
Things about the tool surface that shape how every case has to be written:

  1. The QA mailbox can't create its own inbound mail. send_message only produces mail from the mailbox under test. Two ways around it (see §3.1):
  2. A second, sender mailbox (the maintainer's personal account, through the global mcp-gee-sweet server) sends real mail to the QA mailbox. That gives genuinely delivered messages: a real foreign From, Gmail's own MIME and Message-ID, real spam/category filtering, and two-party threads.
  3. users.messages.insert from a scratch script (the TC-GM23 pattern) for anything send_message can't express: a custom Reply-To, a non-UTF-8 charset, a multipart/related inline image, a pre-labeled SPAM/TRASH message. insert works under gmail.modify; confirmed on PR #815.
  4. No draft cleanup. Resolved by #1205: cases now clean up with delete_draft (TC-GM48–53). Before it there was no list_drafts/delete_draft, so every create_draft that wasn't then sent left a draft behind (via the tools), and cases had to send the draft (TC-GM15) or clean up by script.
  5. No untrash. trash_message is one-way through the tools. Whether modify_labels(remove_label_ids=["TRASH"]) restores a message is unverified; the API has a dedicated untrash endpoint. Test it once (TC-GM37) and record the answer here either way.
  6. No label create/delete. User-label cases need a pre-existing label, which the fixture script creates.
  7. No attachment download. get_message surfaces attachment_id, but nothing can fetch the bytes (out of scope per decision-gmail-domain.md). Attachment cases can only check metadata round-trips.
